articles.title: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 Review - IGN
articles.summary: The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 combines a small generational uplift with AI-powered multi-frame generation to bring along the next generation of graphics cards.
articles.body:
The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 is an odd graphics card . It’s only a bit faster than its predecessor, the RTX 4080 Super , but it’s also significantly cheaper (for now), launching at $999 for the Founders Edition. This makes it not worth the upgrade for anyone who already has a 4080 or 4080 Super, but if you’ve been on the fence waiting for the new generation, you will get significantly better value out of this new graphics card – something that’s far from guaranteed these days.

But the small performance uplift over the RTX 4080, combined with the RTX 5090 ’s weak lead over the 4090 means that Blackwell – the GPU architecture behind these new graphics cards – is one of the least substantial graphics generations in years, at least since Turing and the RTX 2080 Ti. Nvidia is hoping to offset some of that with DLSS 4 and multi-frame generation, which should be genuinely useful to anyone with a high-refresh, high-resolution display, but even then you’re going to have to make peace with some of your frames being generated by AI.

Just like the RTX 5090, the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 is built on the Blackwell GPU architecture, which is especially catered towards AI workloads. Still, it does feature more CUDA cores than its predecessor, with 10,752 spread across seven Graphics Processing Clusters, or GPC, compared to 9,728 cores in the 4080. Also similar to the 5090, Nvidia managed to fit more Streaming Multiprocessors, or SMs into each GPC, which means the RTX 5080 is able to have more CUDA cores without drastically increasing the size of the GPU.

Each of these SMs features four Tensor Cores and one RT Core, meaning you get 336 and 84, respectively. The Tensor Cores, specifically, have been a major focus for Nvidia over the last few years, and Team Green claims these 5th-generation cores are much more efficient, which has paved the way for DLSS 4, at least in part.

The other key behind DLSS 4 and its Multi-Frame Generation is a new AI Manager Processor, or AMP, built directly into the GPU. Essentially, the AMP directs work to different parts of the graphics card, something that was traditionally left to the CPU. But because the AMP is both located physically on the GPU, and is purpose-built for this, it’s able to schedule work much more efficiently than a traditional processor.

The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 also features 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM on a 256-bit bus. That should be enough memory for most people, even at 4K, but games are demanding more and more VRAM every year. With the RTX 5090 packing 32GB of VRAM, it would have been nice to see the RTX 5080 adopt the 24GB featured on the RTX 4090, especially since this GPU is being pitched as a 4K graphics card.

Surprisingly, though, Nvidia hasn’t drastically increased the power demand of the RTX 5080 over its predecessor, requiring 360W, compared to just 320W from the RTX 4080. It’s still an increase, but compared to the monumental 575W needed for the RTX 5090, it’s a modest 13% bump.

That modest power increase means that the Founders Edition has to do a bit less work to keep things cool. Despite that, though, the RTX 5080 looks remarkably similar to the RTX 5090, down to the same gunmetal gray colorway and flow-through heatsinks. It’s little wonder, then, that the RTX 5080 peaked at 77°C in my test suite, compared to 87°C from the same cooler on the RTX 5090. Plus, it’s a dual-slot card, compared to the triple-slot design of the RTX 4080 Super, and still cools better, with the last-gen part peaking at 82W in the same test suite, while only consuming 320W of power.

Rather than monumentally better performance, the big selling point of the RTX 5080 is DLSS 4 , or rather the multi-frame generation part of it. In fact, for the most part, many of the improvements Nvidia is making to DLSS are going to be available on older graphics cards. The improvements that carry over consist of a new AI model that’s going to serve as the foundation of DLSS, moving from the Convolutional Neural Network of DLSS 3 and into a Transformer model.

While the change in the foundational model of DLSS probably won’t affect your frame rate in games too much, it should improve image quality, reducing the ghosting and artifacting that could happen, particularly in older versions of DLSS. But that Transformer model will also help reduce the amount of VRAM needed for DLSS in general, which should help people on lower-end graphics cards push to higher resolutions.

Less of a reliance on VRAM is also what allowed Nvidia to implement MFG, or Multi-Frame Generation on the RTX 5080. Just like the version of Frame Generation that launched with the RTX 4080, MFG works by analyzing a rendered frame, along with motion vector data supplied by the game engine, to generate entirely new ‘AI’ frames between each rendered frame. The big difference here is the scale – MFG allows the RTX 5080 to generate up to 3 frames from each rendered frame in supported games.

Just like the previous version of frame generation, this solution can introduce significant latency, but luckily Nvidia Reflex 2 should help combat it. Just like the original version of Reflex, the sequel zeroes out the render queue provided by your CPU, making it provide frame data just as the frame is about to be rendered. But it takes it further, taking your last mouse position, as well as data from previous frames to more accurately guess where you’ll be moving. That’s combined with hardware flip metering, provided by the AMP, which will pace out the frames to provide for maximum smoothness.

However, all of these solutions can only do so much. In order to get the best experience from multi-frame generation, you’re only going to want to enable it when you’re already getting a decent frame rate. I’d advise only enabling it if you’re already getting 60 fps, or 40 fps if you’re feeling extra frisky.

Once all of that is out of the way, DLSS 4 MFG is actually impressive, at least if you have something like a 240Hz 4K display. In Cyberpunk 2077 at 4K, with the Ray Tracing Overdrive preset and DLSS set to performance, the RTX 5080 was able to deliver 59 fps, right where you’d want it to be. Enable 2 x frame gen, like what’s supported on the RTX 4080 , and that number jumps up to 104 fps. That’s already impressive, but 4 x frame gen sees that number go all the way up to 183 fps – not enough to fully saturate a 4K 240Hz display, but it’s damn close, and you don’t need to spend $2,000 to get there.

Likewise in Star Wars Outlaws , I saw the frame rate go up from a 61 fps average at max settings with DLSS set to performance, up to 100 fps with 2 x frame gen and 176 fps with 4 x frame gen. That means the frame rate essentially triples.

However, because the underlying frame rate remains around 60 fps, you shouldn’t expect a huge increase in responsiveness. The game will essentially just look smoother. That’s not nothing, but it’s not the same as being able to render the game three times faster.

There have been graphics cards in the past that have soared above their predecessors, but the RTX 5080 isn’t one of them. But while it doesn’t have the same kind of uplift that the 4080 demonstrated over the RTX 3080 , it does still provide the best performance you can get in this price range. In fact, this is the second generation in a row where Nvidia’s xx80 card is a legitimate 4K contender for anyone that doesn’t want to sell a kidney for the 5090.

At 4K, the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 is, on average, 11% faster than the RTX 4080, and 8% faster than the RTX 4080 Super, with that performance uplift dropping precipitously at lower resolutions. However, when you add in synthetic benchmarks from 3DMark, that performance differential grows, up to 11% over the RTX 4080 Super and 15% over the RTX 4080. This suggests that this graphics card will get better over time, as new drivers and more demanding games come out.

For this review, I’m using the same comparison data I used for the RTX 5090 last week, along with testing the RTX 4080 and RTX 3080 on Nvidia Game Ready Driver 566.36. The AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX and 7900 XT were tested on AMD Adrenalin 24.12.1. There was an update to Cyberpunk 2077 that launched halfway through my testing process, but I forced DLSS to run on the older CNN model to ensure the results would be comparable. I did not use DLSS 4 or any type of Frame Generation in any of these tests.

In 3DMark, it’s clear that the Blackwell architecture can do some serious work, especially in games with DirectX 12 and ray tracing. In the Speed Way benchmark, the RTX 5080 gets 8,966 points, compared to 7,519 points for the RTX 4080 Super and 7,258 points for the RTX 4080. That makes for a 23% difference over the RTX 4080, not bad considering the 4080 launched for $1,199 – $200 more than the 5080. In Port Royal, a test that focuses heavily on ray tracing, the RTX 5080 also enjoys a 24% lead over the 4080, but it does lose some ground to the 4080 Super, with that lead dwindling to 19%. A sign of things to come.

Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 is a game that naturally rewards high frame rates, and even at 4K, the RTX 5080 is able to get up to 140 fps at the Extreme preset with DLSS set to ‘Performance’. That’s enough for most high-refresh monitors, but compared to the 129 fps from the RTX 4080 Super and 124 fps from the 4080, it’s not exactly a huge leap. And, compared to the Radeon RX 7900 XTX’s 145 fps with FSR set to ‘Performance’, it’s actually a loss compared to the top-end card from Team Red.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the most demanding games on the market, but is getting a lot more accessible as hardware advances. And at 4K with the Ray Tracing Ultra preset and DLSS set to ‘performance’, the RTX 5080 gets 93 fps, compared to 87 from the 4080 Super and 84 from the RTX 4080. That’s just an 11% gen-on-gen improvement from Nvidia in one of its most favorable games.

I test Metro Exodus: Enhanced Edition on the Extreme preset, but without any type of upscaling, because it only supports DLSS, and not FSR. But even without upscaling, the RTX 5080 almost hits the golden standard, netting 58 fps, compared to 53 fps from the RTX 4080. That’s just a 10% generational lead, but still substantially better than the Radeon RX 7900 XTX’s 44 fps in this game.

In Red Dead Redemption 2 , the same problem that plagues the RTX 5090 is present here too, as the game is getting a bit old to be testing high-end GPUs on. In the cowboy simulator, the RTX 5080 gets 127 fps at 4K with every setting cranked up to max on Vulkan. Still, the RTX 4080 Super gets 122 fps and the 4080 gets 120 fps. But, hey, at least it’s a 52% lead over the RTX 3080.

It’s always fun testing Total War: Warhammer 3 because it cuts out a lot of the gimmicks used to sell modern graphics cards. No ray tracing, no DLSS, just pure rasterization. And, well, this ends up being one of the 5080’s strongest showings, getting 92 fps to the RTX 4080’s 76. That’s a massive 21% jump in performance, and close to the potential shown by 3DMark.

It’s funny, then, that I have to talk about Assassin’s Creed Mirage, which shows one of the weakest uplifts for the 5080. In this game, the RTX 5080 is just 4% faster than the 4080, but I suspect this is due to a problem with the driver, similar to the issues I saw in this game when testing the RTX 5090.

Black Myth Wukong is another extremely demanding (and gorgeous) game, but it shows similar scaling to Cyberpunk 2077. In this game, the GeForce RTX 5080 gets 74 fps at 4K with the Cinematic preset, compared to 68 from the RTX 4080, making for a 9% difference. Either way, though, this is good enough performance to flip on frame generation and get much higher frame rates out of it – regardless of how ‘real’ they are.

Finally, in Forza Horizon 5 , I was surprised to see how much faster the RTX 5080 is than its predecessor. The new card gets 171 fps at 4K with the Extreme preset, compared to 146 fps from the RTX 4080 with the same settings. That’s a 17% performance increase, and makes for the best scaling in a game that has DLSS enabled. This also demonstrates that the RTX 5080 doesn’t quite bottleneck my Ryzen 7 9800X3D quite as much as the 5090 does – at least at 4K.

The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 isn’t exactly what I’d call an exciting graphics card, especially compared to previous generations of Nvidia GPUs that just demolished everything that came before. However, while its performance uplift might not be as high as other generations, it’s still an awesome graphics card, especially at 4K. If you’ve been on the fence about upgrading, now might be the time to pull the trigger, especially if you can find the RTX 5080 at its suggested $999 price tag.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: The Wailing Director Returns With Hope, an Uncanny Gonzo Thrill Ride
articles.summary: Hope review: The Wailing director Na Hong-jin returns with a blast of an alien action thriller.
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening from the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Hope will be released in theaters on September 9.

One of the most confounding films to compete for the Palme d’Or, Cannes Film Festival debut Hope is a rip-roaring Korean creature feature made with gonzo skill. Idiosyncratic in structure, spring-loaded with momentum, and doused in additional rocket fuel, it’s the kind of movie sure to divide viewers given how obviously it’s been cut down from something longer and more labyrinthine in scope. However, its flaws are all part and parcel of its dazzling, “How the hell does this even exist?” spectacle. It’s the kind of reaction reserved for bangers like Mad Max: Fury Road , especially given just how much of Hope unfolds on roads and highways at a hundred miles an hour, with characters leaning out of cop cars and practically kissing the pavement; the comparison isn’t unwarranted.

Set along the DMZ in the South Korean border town of Hope Harbor, Hope departs from other great films of its ilk, like Bong Joon Ho’s The Host , by picking a rural setting. Police chief Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min) and various gun-toting locals are called to investigate a bull carcass in the middle of an open road, with claw marks far too big for the local bears, but before they have a chance to dig into the mystery, carnage begins engulfing their nearby township. This thrusts them into utter chaos for nearly the film’s first full hour as they chase down an unseen monster while navigating bodies, debris, and cars sent tumbling from off-screen in scenes that alternate between the dizzying terrors of director Na Hong-jin’s last film, The Wailing , and something out of William Friedkin’s The French Connection , with cameras low to the ground as they zip around tight turns.

While we do eventually see the aforementioned creature – one of several that appear across the movie’s 160 minutes, played via performance capture by Alicia Vikander, Michael Fassbender, Cameron Britton, and Taylor Russell — this initial, extended set piece provides enough heart-in-mouth thrills that you might even wish the monsters remained unseen. Granted, this might also be the case if you’re averse to malformed CGI, but the standards once set by Hollywood aren’t the same everywhere else. The way Na Hong-jin uses his digital tools, as though bringing impossible stop-motion critters to life, makes for a marvelous romp. The characters are largely paper-thin cutouts, but they provide enough levity and allure to keep things moving. For instance, there’s Squid Game mainstay Jung Ho-yeon, who plays rookie cop Sung-ae and gets a heroic, grenade launcher-wielding entrance akin to a South Indian action star.

To say that Hope is an alien film isn’t exactly a spoiler, but discovering the nature of its designs is a delight unto itself. Usually, one look at a movie’s extraterrestrials tells you just how close or far removed its designs are meant to be from humanity, but Hope also features a variety of creatures that make this calculus more complicated. Some of these aliens are elegant, even regal; others are puzzling creations of flesh, bone, and even wood, where you’re never quite sure what you’re looking at (anatomically speaking). Still others feel plucked from the sketchbooks of H.R. Giger, but for the most part, they have just enough human features to place them in the uncanny valley, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing given how they’re used dramatically.

The movie’s most heroic characters – like Zo In-sung’s headstrong, horse-riding tracker, Sung-ki – aren’t those that land the most accurate shots, but rather those that occasionally pause to consider the lives and emotions of these rampaging creatures, catching glimmers of something deeper in their distinctly human eyes. On paper, Hope is entirely a game of figuring out what the f*** the townspeople are even up against, and responding accordingly. But nestled within its action, comedy, and mystery are fleeting moments of empathy that verge on heartbreak for the situation at large, as the movie threatens to become something more sentimental and Amblin-esque.

That it never does is tragic all on its own. You see, Na Hong-jin’s country setting doesn’t just provide wide open spaces for mayhem and detailed production design; rather, it sets the stage for subtle social and political commentary akin to The Twilight Zone and other American Cold War science fiction, drawn from an era when the Red Scare had people seeing communists in their soup. Setting Hope along the border with North Korea has a similar function, between signs that warn not only of animals, spies, and grenades – the alien creatures are, in essence, a combination of the three – but of infiltration at large.

These fears of invasion take shape in kooky ways, like Bum-seok being continually surprised by just how armed-to-the-teeth the people of his town turn out to be. This is funny in the moment, but it speaks to the exact kind of cultural paranoia that breeds the movie’s high-octane violence in the first place. It also seems to breed rot – everything that dies in the movie decays faster than usual, which is never commented upon but ensures that most scenes are drenched in squelching practical effects and buzzing insects. Death is always just around the corner, so every time ammunition tears through the air, it also threatens to make the movie more sickly.

Not since Starship Troopers has large-scale sci-fi action been laced with such wrenching internal conflict, wherein heroes are instantly demythologized and frequent moments offering mutual understanding are dismissed by rattling machine guns. That Hope revels in its violent displays is certainly an attempt to have its cake and eat it too, but Na Hong-jin is more than capable of toeing this tonal line given how unapologetically he drenches each scene in physical and emotional adrenaline. It’s hard not to be swept up by the movie’s deluge of sounds and images.

That the film ends on a note teasing a potential sequel is just as strange as anything you see on screen. However, that Hope also works as an isolated sliver of something larger which we may never see – and which the trigger-happy characters choose not to recognize – feels thematically whole as well. Perhaps the movie’s alleged heroes are too far gone in the direction of selfish survivalism to have ever stood a real chance at building something better and exploring new possibilities, which is nothing if not a warning sign of where we are and what’s to come.

articles.title: The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is the Fastest Gaming Handheld Right Now, but the $1,799 Price Makes It Tough to Recommend When the Xbox Ally X Exists
articles.body:
Ever since the Steam Deck launched in 2022, handheld gaming PCs have been growing steadily more powerful and expensive, and there’s no better example of that trajectory than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. Powered by Intel’s new Arc G3 Extreme handheld chip, MSI’s new handheld is an absolute behemoth, easily able to top 60 fps in some of the most demanding games at its native 1200p, albeit at medium to high presets.

However, this performance comes with a cost. The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ starts at $1,799, making it the most expensive handheld from a mainstream PC maker. Part of that cost can be attributed to AI datacenters driving demand for memory and storage through the roof, but like the Steam Machine earlier this week, the price makes the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ a niche product – at least for now.

Unlike the Steam Machine, though, performance is strong enough on this handheld that anyone looking for the best handheld performance no matter the cost just might want to give the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ a look.

Basically everything is getting more expensive in the face of our current RAM crisis, and handhelds are certainly no different. Just a few weeks ago, the Steam Deck, which had been a budget all-star for years, saw a price rise that put it neck-and-neck with the Xbox Ally. Likewise, the Lenovo Legion Go 2 , which launched at an expensive-for-the-time $1,099 starting price, now starts at $1,499 for its plain Z2 configuration.

It’s unfortunate that MSI has to launch the Claw 8 EX AI+ in this AI-fried market, but the price tag absolutely reflects it. The handheld will set you back $1,799 for its one configuration, netting you the new Arc G3 Extreme processor, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD. That price puts it right up against the now $1,799 Lenovo Legion Go 2, and in that matchup, MSI looks incredible. Because while this new Claw 8 EX AI+ doesn’t have a fancy OLED screen, it’s up to 55% faster than the Legion Go 2.

But the elephant in the room is the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X , which will set you back $999 right now, somehow avoiding the price increases that are hitting basically every other product on the market.

The Claw 8 EX AI+ is much faster than the Xbox Ally X, and even has a larger, brighter display, but it costs nearly twice as much. For most people that just want the best value, the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ just isn’t it right now. But, if all you care about is getting the best handheld performance at any cost, well, it’s hard to argue with the Arc G3 Extreme’s results.

The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ almost looks like someone took the Xbox Ally X and then just stretched it out a little bit. MSI clearly took some notes from Asus’ handheld, with the same controller-like flared grip on the bottom left and right corners of the Claw 8 EX AI+. Honestly, I wish more handhelds would start to adopt this design, because it does feel a bit more natural in hand.

It helps, too, that these flared grips have a nice texture to them, stopping them from feeling slippery after a couple hours of gaming. However, the sheer size of this handheld stops it from being quite as comfortable as the Ally X.

The Claw 8 EX AI+ is 11 inches wide and weighs in at 1.7lb. That’s far from the heaviest, or even the largest handheld I’ve reviewed, with the Legion Go 2 weighing in at a massive 2.03lb. But, unlike Lenovo’s handheld which had comparatively narrower controllers, I seriously have to stretch my thumb a bit to reach the menu buttons on the Claw 8 EX AI+.

The menu buttons are about 3.5 inches up from the bottom of the device, and a little more than 2 inches in from their respective edges. And to add on to the finger-stretching, the buttons are laid out in such a way that the ‘start’ and ‘select’ buttons are further up, while the buttons that bring up the Game Bar and MSI’s software are lower.

I cannot tell you how often I accidentally brought up the MSI Center M software when I just wanted to pull up the map in Crimson Desert . That’s annoying on its own, but for some reason, whenever I dismissed this software, to tab back into the game I was playing, the Claw 8 EX AI+ wouldn’t automatically refocus the game window, which meant I had to tap the screen with my finger to get the controller to work again. Once again, the most annoying part of using a Windows handheld is software.

It’s not all annoying though. The Game Bar button on the left side of the display will bring up a quick settings overlay, where you can swap between different performance modes, as well as toggle a few settings like screen brightness and RGB lighting.

While the rest of the buttons are about what you’d expect on many modern controllers, with the regular face buttons and some back paddles, the Claw 8 EX AI+ has Hall Effect analog sticks and triggers. They feel great right out of the box, and the Hall Effect sensors mean they should last for years before you experience stick drift. I would have preferred TMR (tunneling magnetoresistance) sticks for their improved energy efficiency, especially at $1,799, but hey, I’ll take Hall Effect over a traditional potentiometer sensor.

Along the top of the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ are two Thunderbolt 4 ports, along with a MicroSD card reader and a headphone jack. I love that having a second port has become the norm with modern handhelds, but I would have rather MSI found a way to move one of them to the bottom of the device.

Speaking of the bottom of the device, the Claw’s display extends a bit beneath the rest of the chassis, so that it’s flush with the flared ends of the controller. This design looked wild when I first saw it, but it is growing on me. It allows MSI to use a large 8-inch display while having a smaller chassis than last year’s Claw 8 AI+. I do wonder how durable this display will be over time, but the plastic is more than thick enough to prevent any kind of catastrophic bending.

The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is powered by the new Intel Arc G3 Extreme SoC. This is extremely similar to the Intel Core Ultra 9 388H found in the Asus Zenbook Duo that launched back at CES 2026, but with two of the Performance cores disabled. However, while the CPU was cut back a bit to fit into a handheld’s needs, Intel included the full-fat Arc B390 GPU, with its 12 Xe-cores.

But, really, the biggest difference between the Arc G3 Extreme and the AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme is its age. You see, when the Z2 family launched, it launched with dated architectures for both its CPU and GPU, which meant there wasn’t much improvement over the Z1 Extreme that preceded it. That’s not the case with the G3 Extreme. This is built on Intel’s Panther Lake platform, which is powering all of its current-generation laptops, and it makes a huge difference.

Just compared to last year’s MSI Claw, which was built on Intel Lunar Lake, the Claw 8 EX AI+ is as much as 47% faster in 3DMark Time Spy and 54% faster in Cyberpunk 2077. A lot of that comes down to the Arc G3 Extreme having 12 graphics cores to the Intel Core Ultra 7 258V having 8, but that’s only part of the story.

Even compared to the AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme, the Intel G3 Extreme is a huge improvement. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Claw 8 EX AI+ gets 54 fps at 1080p with the High preset and XeSS set to performance. The Lenovo Legion Go 2, with the same settings, only manages 37 fps. That’s a 37% lead for MSI against a handheld that, at the time of writing, costs the same amount of money.

The Xbox Ally X hurts the Claw 8 EX AI’s value proposition quite a bit, though. While that handheld was tested at 1080p, rather than 1200p, the Ally X gets 44 fps in Cyberpunk at the High preset, with FSR set to Quality. That narrows the Claw’s lead to about 20% – give or take a few points for the difference between 1200p and 1080p – despite its 57% lower cost.

But while the Claw 8 EX AI+ has more raw graphics performance than other handhelds, it also has multi-frame generation. This tech uses the NPU to insert AI-generated frames in between each rendered frame of the game you’re playing.

At its core, this technology isn’t new to handhelds – AMD’s frame gen technology has been available since the Steam Deck. With XeSS frame gen, though, Intel is able to generate up to three AI frames for each “real” frame, which really helps saturate the Claw 8 EX AI’s 120Hz display.

Nvidia famously introduced multi-frame generation as part of DLSS 4 back in 2025, and since then the technology has been controversial, because it can introduce added latency and visual artifacts. The same is absolutely true for Intel’s iteration, but I will say that it feels fine on such a small screen.

Playing Crimson Desert, frame generation brought me from about 40-45 fps to around 155 with frame gen set to 4x. And while that came at the cost of some latency, I didn’t really notice, likely because the game is slow enough for 10-15ms of added latency to not matter all that much. Instead, the game looked a lot more smooth, just by virtue of having more frames sent to the display.

Your mileage will vary, of course, but whether or not you choose to use it, I’d still rather have the option than not.

When Intel was telling me about the Arc G3 Extreme, it said that two performance cores (or P-Cores) were disabled to promote better battery life. And, while that probably did make a big difference, the Claw 8 EX AI+ didn’t fare much better than the Z2 Extreme-equipped handhelds I’ve tested.

In Procyon, which tests battery life through Microsoft Office applications, the Claw did extremely well, lasting a whopping 13 hours. However, when I set a timer and just laid in bed playing Crimson Desert, the battery died after 2 hours and 14 minutes. That’s not worse than I’d expect from the Lenovo Legion Go 2 or the Xbox Ally X, but it’s not exactly better, either. In fact, it falls pretty much right in line with those two devices, which lasted 2 hours and 17 minutes, and 2 hours and 34 minutes, respectively.

However, baked into the G3 Extreme is a new Endurance mode. Basically, when this is enabled, your framerate will be locked to 30 fps (by default – you can configure this in Intel’s graphics utility), and power will be limited beyond that. In games where you’d otherwise get north of 60 fps, this will make a massive difference to battery life, but obviously it’ll have less impact if you’re barely hitting that performance threshold in the first place.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Fans Are More Convinced Than Ever That Robert Pattinson Is Starring in Hideo Kojima’s Physint Game
articles.summary: Robert Pattinson's latest performances in critically-acclaimed films are bringing up an old theory that's gaining more traction as hype builds for Hideo Kojima's Physint game.
articles.body:
Hideo Kojima revealed the first poster for his next action-espionage game, Physint , almost a year ago, along with a handful of casting announcements that confirmed Charlee Fraser, Don Lee, and Minami Hamabe are set to star in the title.

Things have been relatively quiet since then; the most recent update for the game sprouted up in April 2026 in the form of a casting call , with Kojima Productions reportedly on the hunt for an actor to portray a villain with a "German accent."

It’s been months since we’ve heard anything else, and fans are getting antsy… so antsy, in fact, that they’re bringing up an old theory now that a certain actor is making rounds in the limelight.

Ever since Physint’s first poster was revealed, fans have speculated that Robert Pattinson might be involved in the project, with many finding a resemblance between the actor and the shadowy character shown in the poster’s artwork. Those theories intensified after a photo of Pattinson and Kojima went viral shortly after Physint was first announced in 2024.

Now, fans are pointing back to an episode of Kojima’s KOJI10 podcast from 2025, in which the acclaimed game director mentioned that he’d met with Pattinson at an afterparty at the Cannes Film Festival.

"There is a movie called Die, My Love that Jennifer Lawrence is amazing in, and Robert Pattinson is also in the film," he explained. "After the premiere of the movie [in Cannes], there is an after party. And this kind of event gathers a bunch of VIPS and celebrities there, so you absolutely have to have tickets to attend the after party, so I got a few from our agent. But we were short two tickets because there were four of us, and only two had tickets. I was wondering what to do, so I decided to send an email to Robert and he said, 'How many tickets do you need?' and sent the tickets right away."

Kojima went on to describe Pattinson as a "nice guy" and confirmed that he'd spoken with him, though he couldn’t exactly divulge the topic of their conversation.

This podcast episode has picked up speed on social media following Pattinson’s slew of critically acclaimed performances this year; his portrayal of Chris Hansen in Primetime has specifically earned praise from moviegoers, not to mention his work in The Drama opposite Zendaya and Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey alongside Tom Holland and Anne Hathaway.

Commenters are fiending for a Kojima x Pattinson collaboration, with one writing on X/Twitter, "This would be a f**king GENERATIONAL pairing, I want this to be true so bad."

Reminder to people that Pattinson is almost certainly the lead pic.twitter.com/VTVdk8mJ1t

"Pattinson in a Kojima game sounds too good to be true," another said.

"If true, Sony has officially sold me a PlayStation 6, I can’t lie," another joked.

We still likely have a long time to wait until we hear more news about this highly-anticipated title, but in the meantime, fans can check out the latest trailer for his upcoming horror game, OD, which promises to pick up where PT left off.

articles.title: The Live-Action Moana’s 4K Steelbook Is Now Up for Preorder – Here’s Where You Can Grab It
articles.summary: 2026's live-action Moana is making its way to a physical format with a 4K steelbook alongside regular 4K and Blu-ray releases. Here's where you can preorder them, and what bonus features this release comes with.
articles.body:
This year's live-action Moana is sailing the physical media seas to join your movie library this October. As of the time of this writing, a 4K steelbook and Blu-ray copy are available to preorder at select retailers (don't worry, we're keeping an eye out for the non-steelbook 4K, too), alongside a three-film pack on DVD , with each set to be released on October 6.

We've broken down costs and bonus features below, so you can learn more about what to expect with this physical release. It's truly stacked with the latter as well, so if you were a big fan of this live-action reimagining you'll have plenty of extras to enjoy, including a sing along.

Moana (2026) - 4K UHD/Blu-ray Combo + Digital + Steelbook

DVD - Moana (2026), Moana 2, Moana (2016) Multi-Feature Pack (3 Discs)

As mentioned before, only the 4K steelbook and Blu-ray copies have popped up so far when searching around, but we'll be sure to add in information on the non-steelbook 4K once that's available, too. There's also a multi-feature pack on DVD that's available to preorder and comes with the two animated films alongside the new live-action one, if you'd like to own all three in one bundle.

Below, you can get a closer look at the bright and colorful steelbook cover as well, featuring Maui and Moana front and center.

DOLBY VISION/HDR PRESENTATION OF THE FILM

First Light – The journey to making a live-action "Moana" begins. We meet the cast and crew who share what this opportunity means to them and their culture.

It Calls Me – After an extensive search across the Pacific, the filmmakers find their Moana in Catherine Lagaʻaia, a young performer from a Samoan family of artists living in Australia.

Demigod – Dwayne Johnson becomes the first actor to portray both an animated character and its live-action counterpart.

Whole Family Proud – Rena Owen (Gramma Tala), John Tui (Chief Tui) and Frankie Adams (Sina) reflect on portraying the emotional foundation of Moana's world — the family and community that shape her journey.

Motunui – Production designer John Myhre brings together a team of artisans and cultural experts to build the village of Motunui.

Move As One – Choreographer Tiana Nonosina Liufau returns to the world of "Moana" after contributing choreography to the original animated film, this time with the pride of bringing real Polynesian faces and bodies into live-action.

Island Fashion – Costume designer Liz McGregor is tasked with translating the iconic costumes from the animated film into live-action, reimagining them through the lens of traditional Polynesian craftsmanship grounding fantasy in authentic materials and cultural history.

Voices Return – Lin-Manuel Miranda reunites with longtime collaborators Mark Mancina and Opetaia Foaʻi to bring the music of Moana into live-action, reimagining both the original songs everyone loves and a new song "Along The Way."

Mana – Cast and filmmakers reflect on what it means to create a Disney film carried by Polynesian voices, faces and traditions.

Song Selections: "Tulou Tagaloa" "An Innocent Warrior" "Where You Are" "How Far I'll Go" "We Know The Way" "How Far I'll Go (Reprise)" "You're Welcome" "Shiny" "Along the Way (Malaga Ki Ei)" "I Am Moana (Song of the Ancestors)" "Know Who You Are" "We Know The Way (Finale)"

The wait for Moana's physical release isn't long at all, with less than a month to go, but don't let that keep you from preordering early. If you really want the steelbook in your collection, it's always worth it to buy now in case it sells out. And if you're in the mood to buy even more movies while you're on a roll with it, have a look at our rundown of upcoming 4Ks and Blu-rays to see what else is releasing soon.

articles.title: Call of Duty Adds Doom Slayer Skin as Part of New Halloween Update
articles.summary: Call of Duty's upcoming Halloween event will add the Doom Slayer as a playable operator to the game.
articles.body:
Call of Duty's upcoming Halloween event will add the Doom Slayer to the game as a playable operator.

As part of what is expected to be the final season of content for Call of Duty: Black Ops 7, Activision is adding in one of the most iconic protagonists in FPS history: the Doom Slayer. The character will be added as part of The Haunting update, which will be released on September 17. Players will be able to acquire the Doom Slayer operator, inspired by Doom: The Dark Ages, as well as a Doomguy skin which is more in line with the character's look from the original Doom games. Of course, this will all be rounded out with signature Doom weaponry, including the shotgun, crucible blade, and the almighty BFG.

The legendary FPS icon will be added on September 24 via an event pass, which players can purchase. There will also be a free tier which will include various items, such as Doom-inspired skins like a UAC scientist and reseracher, weapon charms, and more. The premium tier will have the Doom Slayer operator skin and the more sought after weapon blueprints.

The Haunting update will include a variety of other non-Doom content, including a nighttime version of the Avalon map, spooky content and foes in Black Ops 7's Endgame mode, limited-time multiplayer modes, and new maps. It's one last hoorah for Black Ops 7 ahead of Modern Warfare 4's release in October, so be sure to hop in and check it out while it lasts.

Black Ops 7 is one of the lesser-recieved Call of Duty games , having launched with a poor campaign and a multiplayer mode that yielded mixed results from the community. The title was partially overshadowed by strong competition such as Battlefield 6 and Arc Radiers, but Treyarch has done its best to support the game with a steady stream of content and updated the game to implement player feedback. The open comms have also rubbed off on Infinity Ward, which has led to Modern Warfare 4 being fine tuned with the community in mind .

articles.title: Trump Administration Tetris Clone Vanishes from White House Website Days After Launch
articles.summary: The Trump Administration appears to have pulled its Tetris clone 'Build the Wall' offline less than one week after its launch.
articles.body:
The Trump Administration appears to have pulled its 'Build the Wall' Tetris clone offline less than one week after its launch .

The title launched last week alongside a small collection of other games as part of yet another attempt from The White House to connect with U.S. gamers. Build the Wall has now vanished from the Arcade.Gov website (as spotted by VGC ), while the four other games it launched alongside it remain.

Those who did try Build the Wall suggested it was clearly aimed to offend, not entertain. Aside from the criticism it received for its subject matter, which asked players to "protect the border from the incoming horde," players quickly realized the game itself didn't seem to be winnable at all. Instead of clearing filled lines, blocks would only continue to fall into place until reaching an inevitable ‘game over’ message when the screen was filled.

We don't know why the Tetris clone has disappeared, but we do know what followed after the Trump Administration launched Arcade.Gov. The website, which was marketed on social media with references to other gaming companies like Nintendo and Sega, quickly resulted in backlash online. The noise grew so loud so quickly that it didn't take long for The Tetris Company to respond.

"At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them," it said. "To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."

P.S. The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall’. P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously. pic.twitter.com/Fu02khRpT3 — Tetris (@Tetris_Official) September 4, 2026

P.S. The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall’. P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously. pic.twitter.com/Fu02khRpT3

Although The Tetris Company also said it takes "copyright infringement very seriously," it did not detail any specific plans to take action against Build the Wall. It elaborated on its feelings in a statement sent to The Verge at the time.

"For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy," it told the site. "The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible. We are currently reviewing the matter."

articles.title: One of Street Fighter 2's Original Designers Wants to Rebalance Super Turbo 3 Decades After Its Release
articles.summary: Akira Nishitani, one of the original designers for Street Fighter 2 and Final Fight, expressed an interest in rebalancing Super Street Fighter 2: Turbo — over 30 years after its release.
articles.body:
Akira Nishitani, one of the original designers for Street Fighter 2 and Final Fight, expressed an interest in rebalancing Super Street Fighter 2: Turbo — over 30 years after its release.

In September 2026 — 32 years after Super Turbo hit arcades in 1994 — Akira Nishitani, a legend in the fighting game world and a veteran of the industry, shared a post on X/Twitter with the wild concept of rebalancing the game after so many years.

“Is it okay to tweak [Super Street Fighter 2 Turbo] again?” he wrote, as spotted and translated by EventHubs. “I wasn't really involved much, but if it's possible, I'd kinda like to give it a shot. Sorry if it turns into a nerf fest, lol.”

スパⅡXを再調整するのアリですか？ 私はほとんど関わっていなかったのですが、もし可能ならやってみたいなぁ。 ナーフ祭りになったらすみませんw — 西谷 亮 (@nin_arika) September 3, 2026

スパⅡXを再調整するのアリですか？ 私はほとんど関わっていなかったのですが、もし可能ならやってみたいなぁ。 ナーフ祭りになったらすみませんw

While Capcom has re-released a slew of its older fighting games over the years for various retro collections, we can’t imagine we’d get a totally rebalanced version of the original SSF2T, one of the most iconic titles in the Street Fighter 2 series. That being said, Nishitani himself believes that it deserves a second pass, though some members of the fighting game community aren’t so sure they agree with him.

For instance, James Chen, a longtime fighting game commentator and fighting game community (FGC) historian, believes such changes wouldn’t be well-received by players, given how beloved the title is and how fondly it's remembered.

“It’s dangerous, as so many love Super Turbo as it is. Many logical changes would be bad, to be honest. Removing, for example, Chun’s ability to store her Super would make her less interesting, while removing Honda’s stored Oicho Throw makes him more interesting (to fight, that is),” he explained.

“SSF2X, despite all the unbalanced stuff, is still a pretty loved game with a pretty active scene despite being +30 years old, so even if you want to balance it, you should be pretty careful with what to change,” another player warned .

It’s also worth noting that Nishitani no longer works at Capcom; he founded his own game development company, Arika, in 1995, where he continues to make games to this day. Fighting game fans might know the studio best for Fighting EX Layer , a spiritual successor to the Street Fighter EX series of the mid-90s.

Capcom has pulled off a few new spins on Super Street Fighter 2 Turbo over the years; in 2008, the company released Super Street Fighter 2 Turbo HD Remix , which was well-received by critics at the time. And in 2017, it released Ultra Street Fighter 2 for the Nintendo Switch, a remixed version of the game with updated graphics, additional characters, and balance changes — but with the current success of Street Fighter 6 , it’s anyone’s guess as to whether or not Capcom is interested in overhauling its original older games once again.

articles.title: PlayStation Architect Mark Cerny 'Nearing the End' of Career, Launching Fellowship Program With Game Awards Creator Geoff Keighley
articles.summary: PlayStation architect Mark Cerny says he's "nearing the end" of his career and wants to pay it forward before he steps away, so he's partnered with The Game Awards creator Geoff Keighley to announce a new fellowship program for game design graduates called the The Nova Games Foundation, with a goal of awarding 20 graduates per year a six-figure grant.
articles.body:
PlayStation architect Mark Cerny says he's "nearing the end" of his career and wants to pay it forward before he steps away, so he's partnered with The Game Awards creator Geoff Keighley to announce a new fellowship program for game design graduates called the The Nova Games Foundation, with a goal of awarding 20 graduates per year a six-figure grant.

Cerny and Keighley spoke to Game File to reveal the nonprofit program, which aims to run for decades, not just years, and promises mentorship to fellowship recipients in addition to the "no-strings" $100,000 grants. The beneficiaries of these awards can earn up to an additional half-million dollars "for projects that are shaping up particularly well." Those determinations will be made based on achieving development milestones.

“I’m nearing the end of my career,” Cerny told Game File's Stephen Totilo. “I’m not done yet, but paying it forward—in the best way possible—is very much on my mind these days.” Keighley added, “I’ve always wanted to give back, but given my role in the industry, I’ve never felt it appropriate to commercially invest in games. I’ve never owned stock in a game company or taken a financial stake in a game. Nova is philanthropy: we aren’t taking equity or looking to recoup the grants. The return we’re hoping for is creative—helping new voices make games and find their footing.”

Hazelight founder and game director on hit two-player co-op games A Way Out (which we loved ), It Takes Two (we adored that one too), and Split Fiction (yup, you guessed it: we think it rocks ) Josef Fares has already indicated his participation via donation and mentorship. Meanwhile, NYU and USC are two of 13 universities from around the world that will be part of the program. The first recipients will be from the classes of 2026 and 2027 from these universities, and they can begin applying in December of this year.

articles.title: 40 Changes We Noticed in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Gameplay Footage
articles.summary: Here are 40 changes we saw when comparing Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 to the N64 version, from things as large as the art style all the way to small menu changes and UI differences.
articles.body:
Nintendo showed roughly 20 minutes of footage from the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time in the Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct this morning . Producer Eiji Aonuma said this project is largely a faithful remake of the N64 classic, reborn on Switch 2 with modern controls and a strong focus on detail. But even though the remake appears to stick closely to the bones of its source material, there are plenty of minor additions and changes I noticed when scrubbing back through the footage for a couple of hours following the Direct.

Here are 40 changes I saw when comparing Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 to the N64 version, from things as large as the art style all the way to small menu changes and UI differences. This list mostly goes in chronological order, starting with the gameplay demonstration from Aonuma and ending with the new trailer that closed the presentation.

A brief warning : I talk in general terms about some items and locations from the original Ocarina of Time. So, if you want absolutely zero knowledge of these things before playing for yourself, stay away!

Obviously, the biggest difference in the remake is its visuals. Aonuma opened his gameplay demo with a look at Kokiri Forest, where the game begins. Everything is more detailed: there are paved stone paths, defined wooden staircases that used to be low-texture ramps, grass blowing in the wind, forest spirits gliding through the air, and modern sunlight seeping through the trees. It's definitely a brand new take on the first 3D Hyrule, especially compared to the 3DS version that essentially just spruced up the original visuals.

Link himself has seen a similarly significant overhaul. We saw lots of Child Link in the gameplay — with snippets of Adult Link showing up in the full trailer later on — and he looks a lot different. His woven green tunic has multiple layers now, with patterns sewn in and flourishes at the bottom. He wears a feather in his hair and has various beads throughout his outfit. I personally love how Link looks now. I think the uncanny art style of the blocky N64 originally shines through brilliantly in this interpretation. We see his mannerisms throughout the gameplay — like stretching when he's left idle for too long, or putting his hands on his hips when speaking to someone — and I think he perfectly embodies the spirit of the Hero of Time.

N64 Ocarina sets you off with a pretty small wallet that can only hold 99 rupees. That's pretty annoying, especially when you open a treasure chest that contains a high-value rupee that you aren't able to fit in your wallet, making it go to waste. On Switch 2, we see Link dive down and grab a blue rupee (worth five, of course) and add it to his wallet, which is shown to have a maximum capacity of 200. I'm sure we'll still upgrade our wallets through the Gold Skulltula questline, but this is a much better start!

On the left side of the new equipment screen, we see a grid of four empty slots (Link just doesn't have the matching items at the start of the game) that appear to be mapped to the top and bottom directional buttons on the left Joy-Con (or the D-pad on the Pro Controller). Later in the gameplay, we see that the Ocarina and Navi are each mapped to one of the left and right directional buttons, but the top and bottom are blank. It would appear that these are going to be shortcuts for equipment earned later in the adventure. I have to imagine this is the solution for swapping boots on the fly (more on that later), but I'm puzzled at what the other slots could be for, given that there are only two special sets of boots to find in the original. We'll have to wait and see.

As Aonuma pointed out, it feels silly to spend time discussing free camera movement in a 2026 game, but it's a huge addition to Ocarina of Time. He demonstrated spinning the camera fully around Link, giving us a look at the poor kid trying to lift rocks for the great Mido. Camera control alone will make the Ocarina remake feel like a significantly different game, especially in stealth sections and tricky platforming moments.

The Direct made a point to emphasize that characters in Ocarina of Time will have a lot more to say. This is one of the changes I'm most excited about: the dialogue text speed in the original is painfully slow by today's standards, and characters don't have a ton to talk about. I'm excited to see how additional dialogue will add to Zelda's characters and world. Even though the remake is largely a faithful adaptation of the original, it's changes like these that will make it incredibly exciting to dive into as someone who's played the N64 version at least a dozen times.

Like the camera control, a dedicated jump button is another mechanical game changer. Jumping is mapped to X — just like the default in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kindgom — and this will surely change how we experience Hyrule. There's a lot of platforming sections in Ocarina's dungeons, and being able to jump and control the camera will do a lot of heavy lifting to make the remake feel modern. I'm a big game feel guy — the weight and maneuverability of a character matters a lot to me — and I'm so excited to zip around Hyrule with the new controls at my disposal.

8. Faster Swim Speed and Altered Swim Meter

Link can also do a little boost to up his swim speed, and I noticed a change to the diving meter's UI. On N64, a three-second countdown timer appeared at the top of the screen when diving. Now, it's a vertical swim stamina bar that appears right next to Link. It's still split into three chunks, so it's likely the same amount of time, but it's a small visual difference.

Aonuma pointed out that the team chose to keep loading screens between large areas to maintain the spirit of the original. But in towns, you can seamlessly walk into stores with no loading screens, which is a huge improvement. We see Link roll right into the shop in Kokiri Forest, which looks similar to entering buildings in Breath of the Wild.

I'm sure Zelda theorists are already hard at work placing every known item from Ocarina of Time onto this newly-designed inventory screen. Based on the Deku Stick's placement in the top left corner, it seems the shape of the background indicates what item goes there. I see a boomerang-shaped icon to the bottom right of the Deku Sticks, three hexagonal shapes that look perfect for the spells you earn from Fairy Fountains, and five slots on the bottom row that look perfect for empty bottles. But aren't there only four empty bottles in the original game? Hmm...

As Link is turning to leave the shop in Kokiri Forest, we see what looks like a training dummy on his left. Not only that, there appears to be an entrance to a back room of sorts next to that, which wasn't present on N64. Maybe some buildings could be slightly expanded?

The combat demonstration in the Great Deku Tree dungeon was one of my favorite parts of today's video. The combat feels even more like a dance with fast-paced choreography — samurai stage shows were one of the biggest influences on Ocarina's original combat, after all — and Link's new animations looked great. He stumbled backwards after a Deku Baba hit his shield, and the slashes feel punchy and impactful, with a bright blast of light to match.

On N64, pressing A in front of a door would cause it to seemingly open automatically without any input from Link. Later 3D Zelda games like Twilight Princess and Skyward Sword animations of Link laboring to lift the door open, and Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is following suit. Inside the Great Deku Tree, we see Link opening doors himself to move from room to room.

14. Crumbling Bridge in the Great Deku Tree

The layout of the dungeons appears to be extremely similar — if not outright identical, it's too early to tell for sure — but there are some small changes within those rooms. In the room where Link finds the slingshot, the original N64 version contains a floating platform that crumbles if Link stands on it for too long. But, he can leap directly off of it to the platform with the treasure chest if he's fast enough. In the remake, that platform is now an entire wooden bridge that stretches all the way to the chest instead of being suspended in midair. It shattered the moment Link stepped on it, forcing him to climb the vines on the side. It's a very small change, but it has me wondering what other differences we'll see in dungeons across the games.

Link can leap while climbing to speed things up, like in Skyward Sword and the open-air Zeldas. Thankfully, there's no stamina meter like in those games, though!

16. Inventory Quick Menu Like Breath of the Wild

Honestly, this was probably my least favorite part of the entire gameplay demonstration. You can open a quick menu to access your entire inventory to equip something on the fly, but it takes the form of a singular horizontal row as seen in Breath of the Wild, Tears of the Kingdom, and Echoes of Wisdom. I'm not a fan of how navigating this menu feels later in Zelda games when you have a ton of items at your disposal, and I think a wheel or customizable shortcut menu would be far more elegant than this clunky solution Nintendo continues to return to.

This has been one of the top changes on my personal wish list: gyro aiming weapons in third person. I love how it feels to fire an arrow in Breath of the Wild, with the added ability to make slight adjustments thanks to motion controls. Aiming appears to work in the exact same fashion in Ocarina of Time: you even use ZR to fire now as opposed to a face button.

This also means you can walk around now while holding your items. The original Ocarina of Time shifted Link to a first-person perspective when aiming, and when you returned to the standard view, Link had put his item away. It's a small detail, but a cute one that really stuck out to me.

Aonuma mentioned that the focus of this remake was strong attention to detail, and that was very apparent during one specific sequence in the dungeon. When Link shoots the ladder down to escape the room where he got the slingshot, the original depicted a ladder stuck in the ceiling that kind of just plops down onto the floor. Now, the ladder is in a stone mechanism, and shooting a switch opens up two paddles that allow the ladder to fall to the ground. This, combined with the bridge that has replaced the floating platform, has me wondering if Nintendo is taking a more "grounded" approach to dungeon design, where everything's placement makes logical sense within the inner workings of the world. A platform doesn't float anymore; it's a bridge. A ladder isn't suspended by nothing anymore; it's locked in place by a stone contraption. I'd have to more closely scrub through the footage to confirm this, but that'd be a really cool mechanical direction for this remake.

The tapestry seen in the June 2026 teaser trailer is now known as the "Threads of Time," a new mechanic to help stuck players figure out where to go. I know Ocarina's main quest sequence ridiculously well at this point, but fully understand that sometimes the game isn't super clear about what's supposed to come next if you don't already know. This seems like a great way for new players to stay on track, and it thankfully seems optional. And, I'm excited to see it get filled in with beautiful art as I progress.

I love the callback to rolling around Hyrule Field to get around faster in the original. Now, holding the button after your initial roll sends Link into a full-on dash, which didn't exist at all before. I think this is perfect: sprinting is expected by modern players, and triggering it with the roll is a nice callback for longtime fans.

Hyrule Castle Town used to be seen through a fixed camera angle perspective, but now it's behind Link's back just like the rest of the game. In my mind, this was an essential modernization to make, and I'm glad Aonuma showed it off in the Direct.

Similarly, the alleys of Castle Town used to be light on detail and actual 3D models. Link took a spin through this part of town, and it's gotten a huge facelift. And, seeing Sakon the thief run through town just made me think it's inevitable that we'll see a Majora's Mask remake with these assets in a couple of years.

One of the most fascinating changes is that time now flows when you're in towns. The passage of time used to pause in places like Castle Town and Kokiri Forest, and only flow in places like Hyrule Field, but now it is always progressing. I'm interested to see how this plays out. Castle Town, for example, used to have two static states: daytime and nighttime. The day was filled with shoppers and people bustling about, while night was relatively quiet. With time now flowing in towns, we're going to see the transition between those two states: people heading in for the night, shops closing down, and so on. I'm excited to see what new interactions that unlocks.

We're getting to the point in this article where the rest of the items on the list are pretty small changes. The Magic Meter in the top left of the screen is now split into more visible sections. That could mean that spells and magic arrow types now have their magic cost specifically listed on the item menu, giving you a better idea of how many uses you have left before you're out of magic.

Just outside of the Castle Town gate in Hyrule Field, I spotted a stone sign or monument I didn't recognize. My first thought was that it's a tombstone that may add lore relevant to Skyward Sword or some other predecessor to the events of Ocarina.

The ocarina songs used to be played on the four C-buttons on the N64 controller, but now they'll be played on the Switch 2's ABXY face buttons as well as L and R. This was the case in the 3DS version, too, but I noticed the patterns more closely mirror the N64's, even though they use the same button layout as 3DS. On Switch 2, Zelda's Lullaby is played with Y-X-A-Y-X-A, which matches the movements of the N64's Left-Up-Right-Left-Up-Right, but differs from the 3DS' X-A-Y-X-A-Y. This is incredibly minor, but if you've made it this far in the article, you probably care about this stuff like I do.

Cutscenes will feature full voice acting in Ocarina of Time, just like in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. And, when running around town, small dialogue bubbles will pop up to show you what Hyrule's citizens are talking about. We saw snippets of cutscenes with Saria, Ruto, Ganondorf, Zelda, and a few others in today's trailer.

Ocarina of Time has integration with the Zelda Notes part of the Nintendo Switch app on smart devices. You'll be able to hunt for specific locations in Hyrule based on screenshots, play Ocarina of Time trivia, play a digital ocarina, and more.

Hyrule Field's size and scope looks extremely similar to the original based on the gameplay and minimap, but some of its topography is different. We see Adult Link running through a swampy area that's far more textured and fleshed out than the original.

We got a brief glimpse of the blue tunic, which has different symbols, textures, and markings on it. Our first look at it is in the Water Temple, where Link uses a hookshot on a far-off target.

Same goes for the red tunic, which slightly differs from the others. Here, it's being worn in the Fire Temple, as Link uses the Megaton Hammer to knock a stone pillar down.

The Water Temple on N64 is notoriously difficult to navigate, especially for first-time players. It has multiple locations where Link can raise and lower the water level to alter the dungeon's floors. To make things simpler, the 3DS version added lights on the walls to help guide you to those water-shifting spots. We can see in the bottom right of the image above that the guiding lights have returned from the 3DS version.

We also see Link instantly take off his iron boots without having to pause and go to the equipment menu. This was a huge pain point in the original — especially in the Water Temple, where you constantly put them on and take them off. Again, the 3DS version fixed this issue, but it's nice to see that carry over to this remake. I actually think the Water Temple is due for a critical reassessment: without the tedious nature of equipping the boots, it's one of my favorite dungeons in the series.

35. A Slightly Redesigned Kakariko Village

We get an overhead look of Link flying through Kakariko Village thanks to a Cucco, and things look a little bit different. It's not too significant, but it seems to me that the house under construction on the right has a slightly different layout. It used to have narrow beams you'd have to carefully tiptoe across, which have been replaced with wider, more forgiving floorboards.

Throughout the gameplay, I noticed that shops were easier to spot in various places. Signs with shields, rupees, and other items were clearly displayed above each building's entrance, from Kokiri Forest to Castle Town. In the image above, you can see Lake Hylia's fishing hole is clearly marked, which was always kind of obscure and difficult to spot in the original.

The snippets of the new soundtrack sound amazing, and it's clearly a fully orchestral score compared to the N64's MIDI tunes. Whether it was flutes in Kokiri Forest, what sounded like a harpsichord in Castle Town, or the heavy dose of strings throughout, I love this early tease of the game's music. Nintendo also released the title track on the Nintendo Music app today, and I've been listening to it on loop while writing this piece.

Amiibo support is coming to Ocarina of Time , with new Young Link and Young Zelda figures coming sometime next year. Scanning them in will unlock a wearable mask based on the N64 models of each respective character, which is actually a pretty fun and silly bonus. I love the Young Link design specifically: Link sitting on a stump with Navi is an iconic piece of Ocarina art recreated for this figure.

39. A Special Edition Console and Controller

On October 29, one week before Ocarina of Time's launch on November 5, Nintendo is releasing the first special edition Switch 2 console themed around The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary. It comes with special Joy-Con 2 controllers and a gold dock featuring the Triforce. There's also a new pro controller and carrying case if you don't need to pick up a brand new console. You can check out all the details on how to preorder the Zelda Switch 2 here .

Finally, in the weirdest moment of the Direct, you can hum the songs Link learns into the Switch 2 microphone, and Link will play them in the game. And it's not just humming or singing: you can play them on a musical instrument, and Aonuma claims the game will pick it up. I'm sure I won't do this besides trying it for novelty, but it's a fun, quirky gimmick that's worth pointing out.

And that's it! I'm sure there is so much more to mine from the trailer and gameplay, but those were my initial takeaways from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. For more, check out all the news from today's Zelda Direct , and don't miss the details on how to watch tomorrow's September 2026 Nintendo Direct . And, check out more of my Zelda thoughts alongside Peer Schneider and Brian Altano on our special NVC episode from earlier today .

Logan Plant is the host of Nintendo Voice Chat and IGN's Senior Editor, Playlist and DB. The Legend of Zelda is his favorite video game franchise of all time, and he is patiently awaiting the day Nintendo announces a brand new F-Zero. articles.title: Every Legend of Zelda Game on the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 in 2026
articles.summary: Every Zelda game you can check out on the Nintendo Switch, plus the new upgrades, games, and features coming to the Switch 2.
articles.body:
The Legend of Zelda is one of the most iconic video game series of all time. Starting on the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1986, The Legend of Zelda follows various incarnations of Princess Zelda and Link as they fight to save Hyrule from the evil that is Ganon. While the series has always been popular, the Nintendo Switch has catapulted Zelda into one of Nintendo's best-selling properties with landmark titles in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Echoes of Wisdom released toward the end of the original Nintendo Switch's life cycle, but Nintendo has already revealed quite a bit about the next generation of adventures in Hyrule. Here's every Legend of Zelda game on the Nintendo Switch as well as new Zelda games coming to the Switch 2 .

How Many Zelda Games Are on Nintendo Switch?

In total, five Zelda games, three Hyrule Warriors games, and one spin-off game have been released specifically for the Nintendo Switch . This includes both mainline entries and spinoff games that were released from 2017 to 2026. All of these Zelda games are playable on the Switch 2. The Ocarina of Time remake, releasing this November , will be the first Zelda game exclusive to the newer console.

All Zelda Switch Games in Order of Release Date

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild - 2017

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild was the first Zelda title released for Nintendo Switch. Launching alongside the system, this title marked a turning point in the Zelda series, bringing a style of open world gameplay that we'd never seen before. You can traverse to anywhere you can see in the world. Link awakes after a 100 year slumber, where he is tasked by the spirit of Hyrule's former King to save Princess Zelda from Calamity Ganon - a primal evil trapped inside Hyrule Castle.

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild - Nintendo Switch

Hyrule Warriors: Definitive Edition - 2018

Hyrule Warriors is an action hack and slash title developed by Omega Force and originally released for the Wii U. Characters from all kinds of Zelda games make an appearance, whether as playable characters or villains. The game was brought over to Nintendo Switch in 2018 in the form of Hyrule Warriors: Definitive Edition, and includes all characters, stages, and modes from the original game in addition to Breath of the Wild inspired costumes for Link and Zelda.

Hyrule Warriors: Definitive Edition - Nintendo Switch

Cadence of Hyrule is an extremely unqiue collaboration between Brace Yourself Games and Nintendo. The game combines the roguelike rhythm gameplay of Crypt of the NecroDancer with the world of The Legend of Zelda and its characters. This spinoff offers an incredible soundtrack and beautiful pixelated graphics. Up against Octavo, a musical villain, Zelda and Link team up with Cadence to thwart his plans and save the Hyrule.

The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening - 2019

The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening is a remake of 1993 Game Boy title developed by Grezzo. This charming platformer sees Link castaway at Koholint Island, where he must solve the mystery of the Wind Fish, a legendary being said to be on the island. Unlike some of the more modern Zelda titles, Link's Awakening takes you across many different dungeons and areas to collect the Instruments of the Sirens. If you never got the chance to play the original Link's Awakening, this is the definitive way to experience one of the Zelda series' most unique titles.

The second Switch entry in the Hyrule Warriors series, Age of Calamity is set 100 years before the events of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. Here, you can experience firsthand the events that occured in the fight against Calamity Ganon. All of your favorite Breath of the Wild cahracters are here and playable, including Link, Zelda, the Champions, and so many more. Omega Force created a fun and expansive title, with two waves of DLC you can check out after completing the main story.

Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity - Switch

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD - 2021

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD is the long-awaited remaster of the classic Wii game . Set at the beginning of the Zelda timeline, Skyward Sword takes Link to the skies as he traverses across the world to save his childhood friend Zelda. You'll uncover the Master Sword was created as part of this journey, among other things. The remaster includes the iconic motion controls you can operate with the Joy-Con and a new button-only gameplay style for those looking to play without motion.

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD - Nintendo Switch

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - 2023

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom hit the market in 2023, selling over 10 million copies in just three days as well as quite a few special edition Switch consoles . Set a few years after the events of Breath of the Wild, Link is tasked once again with finding Princess Zelda after Ganondorf is resurrected. Tears of the Kingdom takes to both the skies of Hyrule and the depths below the land. This creates one of the largest maps you'll find in any game, leaving for hundreds of hours of exploration to be had. All in all, it's the best Zelda game of all time and a hard one to follow.

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Nintendo Switch

The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom - 2024

But, of course, Tears of the Kingdom was not the end of this beloved Nintendo franchise on the original Switch. The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom was announced during the June 2024 Nintendo Direct before launching on the Switch in the fall later that year. While Echoes has the titular Princess take the story's reigns, and features a more 2D art style à la Link's Awakening, it should not be mistaken as a spin-off or side project. This is a full-blown, magical Zelda game, that lets you unlock your creativity to try and save Link and the rest of Hyrule in entirely new ways.

The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom - Switch

Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment - 2025

The latest Zelda-adjacent release is a new entry in the Hyrule Warriors series. Nintendo has heavily emphasized that the story is canon, giving us a deeper look at the Imprisoning War in what is essentially a prequel to Tears of the Kingdom. You get to play as a spread of different characters , including Princess Zelda, who has been sent into Hyrule's past and must work with new allies in the fight against Ganandorf.

Available Zelda Games With Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack

If you're interested in checking out some of the older Zelda titles, the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack service has loads of Zelda titles from Nintendo's older consoles. Here is every Zelda game currently available on the service:

The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past - Four Swords

The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening DX

*On the GameCube library exclusive to the Switch 2

There hasn't been any word on new mainline Legend of Zelda games... unless you count a pretty massive Ocarina of Time remake . Yep, it's real, and it's coming to Switch 2 on November 5. We got a pretty good look at the new graphics and gameplay in a recent Nintendo Direct dedicated entirely to the Zelda franchise . The Ocarina of Time remake is now up for preorder as a Switch 2 exclusive, and is being accompanied by a new Zelda-themed Switch 2 console and Pro controller .

In addition to the games themselves, Nintendo has also announced they will be bringing Hyrule to the big screen with a live-action Legend of Zelda movie . In terms of details, the movie's director, Wes Ball (Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes), has expressed his desire to make a more "grounded" Zelda adaptation that feels like live-action Miyazaki . The Zelda movie will be releasing in theaters on March 26, 2027 and Nintendo has officially confirmed the actors playing both Link and Zelda.

See the full list of upcoming Switch games for everything coming to the system.

Noah Hunter is a freelance writer and reviewer with a passion for games and technology. He co-founded Final Weapon, an outlet focused on nonsense-free Japanese gaming (in 2019) and has contributed to various publishers writing about the medium.

articles.title: Snoop Dogg Biopic Casts D'Angelo's Son, Swayvo Twain, as The Notorious B.I.G.
articles.summary: Snoop Dogg's biopic has cast Swayvo Twain, the son of D'Angelo, as Notorious B.I.G.
articles.body:
Snoop Dogg's biopic has cast Swayvo Twain, the son of D'Angelo, as The Notorious B.I.G.

The Snoop Dogg biopic, simply titled Snoop, was announced in 2022, and is now ramping up for release next summer. Over the last couple of months, the film has added a number of actors to its cast to play legendary rappers like the titular musician himself, Nate Dogg, Dr. Dre, Tupac, and more. The movie is comprised of a mostly unknown/up-and-coming cast, which now includes Swayvo Twain, the son of D'Angelo.

Swayvo Twain will play one of the all-time great hip-hop artists, The Notorious B.I.G., in the film. It's unclear how much screen time he'll have in the actual movie itself, but he obviously played a big role in the rise of rap in the '90s. Snoop Dogg and Notorious B.I.G. were heavily involved in the East-Coast-West-Coast rivalry, which will almost certainly play a role in the movie. The film is being directed by Craig Brewer, who helmed 2025's Song Sung Blue and 2005's Hustle and Flow.

Snoop Dogg himself is having a pretty active time in the entertainment industry as a whole. The rapper is the current elusive target in Hitman and will play an original character in the Yakuza prequel, Stranger Than Heaven, next year. Tupac's likeness is also being leveraged for a different character in that title .

Snoop is expected to hit theaters on August 6, 2027.
