articles.title: Sony isn’t phasing out discs quite as quickly as we thought
articles.summary: Sony’s last discmaking plant is reportedly decreasing production by 10 percent, not 90.
articles.body: Sony isn’t backing away from its decision to kill the video game disc in January 2028. But Sony isn’t shutting down production as quickly as we thought, either. Two months after reports that Sony’s last discmaking plant was already being repurposed, the company’s discmaking division now says that one widely reported detail was wrong. Originally, it sounded like the division’s president said the Thalgau plant would produce 90 percent fewer discs in 2028 — but the reality is it will only produce 10 percent fewer discs in 2028, an unnamed Sony DADC spokesperson told Game journalist Brian Crecente. “To clarify and avoid any misleading information: in that statement Dietmar anticipated an overall product volume decline by 10 percent, not a decline down to 10 percent,” the spokesperson said. Sony DADC did not respond to The Verge’s fact-check request, including our question about whether the division is still restructuring and retraining every single one of the plant’s 300 employees to work on microlenses instead of discs, as ORF Austria reported in July. It wouldn’t tell Crecente any more details, either. One reason that the discmaking plant might take longer to transition: Even if Sony won’t produce brand-new games on disc after the January 2028 cutoff, the company will continue to let publishers “place re-orders for existing PlayStation disc games.” Even if PlayStation discs stick around longer than we thought, the future isn’t looking good for the concept of video game ownership. Several major game publishers are conspicuously missing from Microsoft’s disc-to-digital initiative, and Sony keeps giving gamers reason to believe it doesn’t respect the idea of ownership at all. Most recently, Sony made the breathtakingly blunt legal argument that “reasonable consumers” couldn’t possibly believe they own a game after they buy it — because if they truly owned a game, how could multiple copies exist at a time?

articles.title: Breaking Benjamin Frontman Stops His Own Concert to Rant About His Feud With a Fallout 4 Modder
articles.summary: Benjamin Burnley, lead singer and guitarist of the rock band Breaking Benjamin, took five minutes during a concert in Holmdel, New Jersey, to rant about his feud with a fellow Fallout 4 modder.
articles.body:
Benjamin Burnley, lead singer and guitarist of the rock band Breaking Benjamin, took five minutes during a concert in Holmdel, New Jersey, to rant about his feud with a fellow Fallout 4 modder.

If you didn’t know Benjamin Burnley was a big gamer, now you do. He announced this information during a concert on Sunday, September 6, revealing that he’s an “amateur modder” for Skyrim and Fallout 4.

Lately, he’s been beefing with a fellow modder over a mod he recently created for Fallout 4 that allows users to play the game in first-person. He thinks it’s a pretty solid mod — but the other guy just doesn’t see the vision.

Fallout 4: Anniversary Edition Screenshots

His spiel was caught on video by a fan at the concert, who posted footage of the moment on Reddit under the name ‘im_all_ears.’

“I just made a mod that makes it so that when you’re in first-person, you stay in first-person. You see your body in first-person. You go to your workshop area in first-person, and third-person still works. So, I want you to go and download that f**kin’ mod,” Burnley began.

“More importantly, I wanna tell you why I’m doing this. There was a modder — so, there’s like a clique, there was a modder in the community that was really mean to me and bullying me and saying, ‘Oh, you mod is sh*t, you don’t know what you’re f**kin’ doing, so I'm doing this every fucking night, and blowing his fucking downloads out of the water. Please help me destroy this f**kin’ jerk. I’m not even gonna say his name, but he’s a d**k, and f**k him.”

Production even posted the name of the mod on the venue’s big screen, along with Burnley's Nexus Mods username: “ True First Person Mod by killemloud.”

“Even if you don’t play that game, go download it. It’s on Nexus Mods,” he urged. “And tomorrow, I better see all those downloads going up. …This is for people who love mods. I’m uploading the update for it. You know, when you post a mod, you’re supposed to be able to grow and learn, and make it better. And right off the bat, this f**kin’ a**hole was s**tin’ on my mod, and he ain’t lettin’ me update it. So that’s what happened.”

While there were quite a few gamers in the crowd who couldn’t get enough of this humorous feud, one or two vocal fans yelled at Burnley to “play some music” rather than rant about Update 1.2 for his first-person mod. The entire spiel took nearly five minutes, and it has since gone viral across social media for the reasons you might expect.

“No way Ben makes Fallout 4 mods, that's insane lol,” one wrote on Reddit.

“Benjamin Burnley makes gaming mods?! The f**k? That’s awesome!” another said.

Breaking Benjamin was also famously featured in Halo 2, but there’s oodles of celebrity gamers out there; most recently, Obsession star Inde Navarrette went viral for having a Twitch channel, where she streamed games in the Call of Duty series and story-based titles like The Last of Us , while Samara Weaving — recently cast as Emma Frost in Marvel’s upcoming X-Men movie — received praise for being such a hardcore gamer that she takes her PlayStation 5 with her on the road while she’s filming movies.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: The First Dungeon Crawler Carl Graphic Novel Is a Great Read, Even if You've Already Read the Books
articles.body:
I've been a fan of Dungeon Crawler Carl for years now. I've read all of the books and listened to the audio versions , so the obvious next step for me was to pick up a copy of the first graphic novel. Having experienced Matt Dinniman's story multiple times already, my biggest concern going into the graphic novel adaptation is that it wouldn't feel additive. But despite a few minor issues, I can honestly say it is an awesome way to experience Carl and Princess Donut's chaotic integration into Dungeon Crawler Carl World.

Dungeon Crawler Carl, Vol. 1 (Graphic Novel)

The first thing you'll notice, from the cover alone, is the art style. Carl and Princess Donut are drawn to look like manga versions of themselves with big eyes and exaggerated expressions. For the most part, I really liked how Laurel Pursuit Studios decided to portray this universe. There are a lot of crazy creatures down in the dungeon, and each and every one of them looks like they belong in anime. With the Dungeon Crawler Carl TV series making the decision to go live-action , this graphic novel is a neat look into what it would look like if they'd decided to go in an animated direction instead.

All of the things that make the art style great are also what hold the story back at times, however. Carl has a generally grumpy or angry expression throughout (which makes sense), but occasionally the illustrator will show pops of gleeful madness that I don't think belong in the story just yet. It felt a bit like they were trying to showcase too wide of a range of emotions than were strictly necessary for book one Carl.

With that being said, I think the studio did an excellent job of adapting the parts of the books you wouldn't actually see. You don't get nearly as much of Carl's inner monologue in this format, so all of that has to show up in how he's drawn and interacts with the world instead. This translates beautifully into how combat and dialogue are portrayed, only stumbling when I felt my mental image of the characters differed slightly from what I was seeing. In most instances, though, I felt like the graphic novel was able to add a depth to the story I'd never been able to get with the books themselves. Questions like "What does a Bopca actually look like?" are answered here and it just feels right.

Seeing as this is an adaptation of a LitRPG series , I was also thoroughly impressed at how well system messages were incorporated into the story. Pop-ups about achievements, rewards, and AI nonsense are initially shown as a completely overwhelming experience before getting neatly integrated in between panels. The AI is such an integral part of the story, but I could see how some of the lengthier messages it sends throughout the story could feel bloated on the page. The way it was done here felt totally seamless.

The first volume of the series collects the first 13 chapters of the ongoing Webtoon series, which equates to about a third of the first book. Without spoiling anything for anyone who hasn't read the book, I can tell you that the ending of volume 1 doesn't feel abrupt. The story hits its first major high note and you get just the right amount of cool-down time before setting up a part 2. You can already read more of the story for free on Webtoon , or wait for Volume 2 to arrive on October 6 for that paperback experience.

articles.title: Artificial Looks Like a Horror Movie in First Teaser for Sam Altman Biopic After Amazon Pulled the Plug
articles.summary: Neon has unveiled the first teaser for Luca Guadagnino's Sam Altman biopic, Artificial, after Amazon abruptly canceled its support for the film earlier this year.
articles.body:
Neon has unveiled the first teaser for Luca Guadagnino's Sam Altman biopic, Artificial , after Amazon abruptly canceled its support for the film earlier this year.

With the director behind Challengers at the helm and a star-studded cast, the first teaser for the OpenAI movie somehow manages to surprise. In a little more than a minute, the trailer promises a tense look into Altman's life that leans heavily on the horror vibes, with the video teasing a peek behind the curtain into the events that led to the creation of controversial tech tool ChatGPT.

Altman, played by Andrew Garfield (The Social Network, The Amazing Spider-Man), can be seen walking through dark corridors backed by eerie strings before reaching a blue-lit room loaded with guns. It looks like the kind of saferoom the OpenAI CEO teased he might have when speaking to The New Yorker in 2016, but the horror elements come from more than the visuals. His character can be heard whispering lines, including "We opened Pandora's box together" and "We get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world."

Garfield walks, talks, acts, and even looks like Altman in the first trailer for Artificial, but he's far from alone. Monica Barbaro (A Complete Unknown, Top Gun: Maverick) also shows up in the movie and its first teaser trailer as former OpenAI executive Mira Murati.

Cooper Hoffman (The Long Walk), Yura Borisov (Anora), Jason Schwartzman (Scott Pilgrim vs. the World), Mark Rylance (Bridge of Spies), and Chris O'Dowd (Bridesmaids) also have their own roles to play in Guadagnino's retelling. The role many viewers are likely already keeping an eye out for, though, is Ike Barinholtz's (The Studio) Elon Musk . Quick flashes of the Tesla boss do appear in the trailer, but they do little to tell watchers what to expect from his portrayal in Artificial.

Despite the star power and talent behind it, Artificial very nearly never came to be. Amazon was previously attached to release the project but chose to cut its involvement in June 2026, just three months ago. The move allegedly came just after multiple private test screenings for the nearly complete movie, leading to confusion amongst fans of Guadagnino's work. Amazon's decision to drop Artificial also happened to arrive only a few months after the company committed to a $50 billion investment in OpenAI .

Artificial was dropped by Amazon and eventually picked back up by Neon . It's now set to come to select theaters Christmas Day 2026. For more on OpenAI, you can read about how the tech company shut down its generative AI app Sora earlier this year.

articles.title: Exodus: Five Things You Need to Know
articles.summary: Exodus: Five Things You Need to Know
articles.body:
We’re rapidly approaching three years since the world got its first look at Exodus. A lot has happened in the world since 2023 - many games have come and gone in the span between. It would be fair to question if Exodus has kept pace with the movements of the market.

Happily, all this time has gone to good use. Developer Archetype Entertainment, backed by legendary tabletop game publisher Wizards of the Coast, are now on the downhill run on this science fiction sprawler and it’s finally time to wrap our mitts around a gamepad and get stuck in. Archetype is rightly avoiding Grand Theft of Your Time in November and touching down on April 7, 2027 instead, so now’s the perfect time for a progress check-in.

Here are Five Things You Need to Know about Exodus.

Exodus’ story focuses on the practical and sometimes heartbreaking effects of time dilation, where days of interstellar space travel for the player mean decades passing for loved ones back home.

Players take on the role of “Traveler” Jun Aslan, this game’s Commander Shephard, but with heartthrob hair and a charming disposition. He is the stalwart son of famed veteran Traveler, Orion Aslan, but through happenings as yet unclear, Jun starts the game as a humble salvager on a dying world overrun by a technovirus known as The Rot. To save your planet, which every good hero should aim to do, you must reclaim your father’s legacy and stop The Rot.

Still with me? Good. The Rot, as we understand it, is a byproduct of The Celestials: descendants of the first humans. They’ve evolved far beyond humanity’s capabilities - around 40,000 years more advanced, and are a persistent threat to humanity’s continued existence in Exodus.

To further complicate things, Jun is also a genetic crosspoint of sorts; he can, for reasons still unclear, interact with Celestial technology, imbuing him with special active abilities - sort of a techo-blend of Psy attacks and quasi-magical spells (but I’m sure the game has detailed lore that will explain the context better than I can). In practice, just like Mass Effect, you’ll be upgrading these abilities throughout the journey, triggering all sorts of cool effects, environmental modifiers, attacks, defensive techniques and so on.

2. THE UNIVERSE IS FULL OF “AWAKENED” BEINGS

The team allowed us to play through one mostly complete mission on PC, abridged in a couple places to keep the pace moving (and presumably to cut minor story moments). We meet our swarthy hero Jun Aslan aboard his sleek vessel (reminiscent of the N7, in fact), joined by a multi-racial, multi-species crew.

Let’s talk about The Awakened. The universe is teeming with animals, as it turns out. The Awakened are animals have been granted human intellect through some means, and this is a very good thing for players, because in addition to all sorts of interesting alien races, you can now expect some brilliant dealings with all kinds of talking critters, and oh boy, they all have plenty to say about how cruddy and exploitative humans generally are. They’re not wrong!

The team have revealed eight of Jun’s companions so far - and teased that there are still some to be revealed. The current roster includes: Tom Vargas, Elise Charroux, Phaedra Nath, Salt, Houston, Suliman, C.C. Orlev and Emrys, but alledgedly there are 11 crew to find. One standout is an Awakened anthropomorphic wolf named Houston, who, curiously, is your adopted brother.

The recent Gamescom trailer also introduced us to Salt - a blunt, bounty-hunting Awakened Octopus in a mech suit. She is a sniper who can use her ink as a smokescreen to provide cover in combat.

As an aside, it seems like Octopi are having their moment, perhaps propelled into popularity through the 2020 film “My Octopus Teacher”. Then came The Boys’ romantic (albeit warped) relationship between an octopus and The Deep. I digress, but in Exodus, you can look forward to meeting lots of Awakened species, tentacled or otherwise.

Back to the mission, and Jun’s goal is to set down inside the hangar bay of a large orbital space station that houses a race of Awakened Frogs known as the Kay from the planet Lidon. The Kay have been exploited and driven into exile - but all is not lost! One Kay, catchily named 42C, has developed a soft spot for human music - thumping heavy electronica - and is eager to help guide you.

Your offside for the mission is the equally swishy-haired, but slightly stiff Suliman: a dark-eyed representative of a powerful faction that Jun must align with. Why? Because their support will enable you to get your hands on some critical parts that will allow your ship to travel between star systems. There’s no free lunch, even in the cold of space.

Anyway, the opening sequence lets us appreciate the gorgeous facial animations delivering engaging and nicely performed dialogue sequences from decorated Narrative Director and writer Drew Karpyshyn and his team of ex-Bioware, Naughty Dog and 343 alumni. Again, there’s an instant fee ling of Biowaresque familiarity, thanks to a sharp script, infusing the characters and scenarios with plenty of personality.

In practice, it’s clear the team has studied what makes the genre leaders successful. Mass Effect’s team directing mechanics are implemented almost identically, for one. That’s a good thing, insofar as I was able to jump into a mission that takes place a couple hours into the start of the game and not feel completely overwhelmed.

We start in a micro-gravity environment, making our way into the guts of the ship. Jun can sprint, jump, grapple, dive behind cover, roll and dodge attacks, and scale up ledges. Jun’s an agile fella and you’ll rarely feel constrained.

In true action-RPG form, you’ll be spending a good portion of time dealing out commands to your squad in slowed-down time. The radial menu pops up and pumps the brakes on the game speed, allowing you precious seconds to target enemies and queue up your squad’s preferred attacks and manoeuvres. You can, of course, just duke it out guns akimbo, but the game urges you to play around with a raft of abilities: aerial bombardments, stealthy teleportation attacks and such. These squad attacks can be timed up for combo damage too, which is a nice touch.

We pushed forward through hallways and tunnels, activating mechanical ledges, grappling up platforms and activating switches. You’ll be collecting resources, crafting ammo, unlocking new items, weapons and skills as you do. It’s what you’d expect in a game of this nature, and so far, Exodus is delivering the goods.

Eventually we meet up with a couple of Awakened Frogs, who compel you to help them - and put you at odds with Suliman at times. The story doesn’t shy away from dark themes and puts you in positions that force you to make hard decisions. Do you sell out an entire species for immediate gain, or risk it all and keep your chin held high?

Later, I came upon an injured enemy and I was posed with further ethical dilemmas. Yes, you’ll be choosing from morally grey responses to many situations and your teammates will judge you based on how just firm your backbone is. In Mass Effect, you were leaning towards Paragon or Renegade. In the Exodus-verse, your choices put you in either “Paladin” or “Immortal” baskets. I’m a softie (Paladin), because I like to help the injured, rather than doom them - but you do you.

It is nice to see a return to branching dialogue trees and vastly different outcomes. I won’t spoil the mission’s various encounters, but I had a great time trading barbs with an uptight robot and the game certainly rewards you for being ruthless.

The mission culminates in a final ethical quandary - and the whole situation devolves into a down and dirty fight with a gigantic Awakened Grizzly Bear. Yes, you’ll fight space bears. Be still my heart. It’s a great demonstration of the importance of mastering your abilities and coordinating your squad - but I did feel bad killing the bear. I guess you’re supposed to.

I played through this mission twice and explored the different outcomes - but both resulted in a messy end for one particular character, so the game definitely steers you towards certain outcomes. Regardless, you’ll have a great time along the way. Hopefully there’s room for some diplomacy now and then for the pacifists out there.

Our time with Exodus was brief but tantalizing. Questions remain around the time dilation concept, for all the sales pitching around that feature. I’m also unclear on the overall structure of the game - which I feel is integral to selling the epic setup. Just how linear is the story? Are there more space bears? These are the big questions.

Undeniably, the game shows a lot of promise. Terrific production values throughout, a great score punctuated by weapon fire that chimes and beats in time with the music. Little touches like that stood out to me more than the almost-textbook gameplay implementation. I suspect there is a hell of a lot more under wraps though and I look forward to rolling back those covers.

“Space opera” is a term that gets bandied around, sometimes at a stretch, but Exodus arguably deserves the moniker. In my mind, operas demand a certain emotional depth or resonance with the audience; the story is about the characters in the universe, rather than the science and technology propelling them forward. Exodus has plenty of the latter of course, but the interplay matters just as much.

What we’ve seen and played so far is shamelessly like Bioware’s take on action-RPGs and far flung universe-building. I cannot wait to keep playing this. Playing through, I didn’t realise just how much I missed this style of intelligent RPG-forward storytelling in an atmosphere of hardened science fiction gunplay and strategy.

With a bona fide new Mass Effect installment coming in the next couple years (talk about a broad window), there’s plenty of time for Exodus to pull in a swathe of fans looking to lose themselves in the infinite void.

articles.title: The Bomb Busters Board Game Drops to Its Lowest Price Ever at Amazon
articles.body:
Bomb Busters is now 30% off at Amazon for a limited time, which is the lowest price we've ever seen on the cooperative board game. It has been just over a year since this game was named the 2025 Spiel des Jahres in Germany, the highest honor in board games.

For those not familiar with the German "Game of the Year" award, it's a pretty big deal in the tabletop community. After news of its win broke, the game sold out pretty much everywhere in North America. If you don't already have it in your collection, this discount makes it a great time to pick it up.

As for what type of game Bomb Busters actually is, you can look to the name for answers. It's a strategic cooperative board game that sees 2-5 players attempting to diffuse a bomb and cut the correct wires. There are a total of 66 different missions included, with increasing levels of difficulty. If you've ever played the video game Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes , you should have an idea of what to expect.

All-in-all what makes Bomb Busters great is that it's something anyone can play. It's a great board game for families or to pull out with a small gathering of friends. Typical games will only take around 30 minutes to play, so you can quickly work together to diffuse a bomb and then move onto something else if you want.

While Bomb Busters won last year's award, it's worth pointing out that the runner-up is also an excellent game. It's a fun and fast-paced card game with an incredibly affordable price tag. Similar to Bomb Busters, gameplay is quick and easy to learn. IGN gave it a 9 out of 10 in our review , calling it "an easy recommendation regardless of your experience with card games, the size of your collection, or even your age."

articles.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Is Finally Getting a 4K Blu-ray Release Ahead of Season 3
articles.summary: The Rings of Power is finally getting a 4K Blu-ray release ahead of the Prime Video show's third season.
articles.body:
The Rings of Power is finally getting a 4K Blu-ray release.

The Prime Video series inspired by J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of The Rings has been a streaming exclusive since it first premiered back in 2022. Now, Amazon has revealed a spread of 4K Blu-ray releases for both seasons of the show, including some particularly gorgeous limited-edition steelbooks.

All of the DVD releases are now available to preorder ahead of their release dates in November and December, which will roughly coincide with the release of the show’s third season .

The Rings of Power Now Up for Preorder in 4K Blu-ray

The Rings of Power Season 1 [Limited Edition 4K Steelbook]

The Rings of Power Season 2 [Limited Edition 4K Steelbook]

Both seasons of The Rings of Power are getting the same general breakdown of DVD releases. Your options, listed in order from the cheapest to the most expensive, are a standard DVD ($39.99), Blu-ray ($46.99), and 4K ($51.99), as well as Amazon-exclusive limited-edition 4K steelbooks ($61.99). The standard DVDs for both seasons will all be released on November 3, while the limited-edition steelbooks won’t ship until December 1.

The standard DVDs for Season 1 all feature the same cover art. You get a look at most of the main cast, though the focus is on Galadriel against the bright white background.

The 4K steelbook for this one has some fantastic old-school fantasy vibes, coming in a gold slipcase with frames images of Galadriel on the front and the Great Tree on the back. The steelbook also comes with six collectible art cards, each featuring some ethereal photographed portraits of individual characters.

The Season 2 Blu-ray cover art takes the spotlight away from Galadriel and instead points it almost toward Sauron. It also goes with the black background, having generally “darker” vibes than its first season companion.

Along similar lines, the 4K steelbook for Season 2 swaps out the gold slipcase for black, and the small image of Galadriel for a darker still of Sauron. The back of the slipcase shows off a forge. The full steelbook also comes with six more collectible art cards, this time featuring particularly action-packed and rugged poses.

The Rings of Power is returning for its third season on November 11, 2026. Because it’s been so long since Season 2, Prime Video has already confirmed the new season will kick off with a “Fellowship-style" prologue before diving into some tense battles and introducing new characters . While the show will once again stream exclusively on Prime Video , it will presumably get its own 4K Blu-ray release at some point in the future.

articles.title: SteelSeries Aeon Pro Review So Far
articles.summary: The SteelSeries Aeon Pro packs in just about every "pro" feature you could ask for in a controller, with Hall-effect thumbsticks, tactile switch buttons, adjustable triggers, and the company's outstanding hot-swappable battery system.
articles.body:
The SteelSeries Aeon Pro is one of the most advanced controllers I've ever tested. It's also the most expensive – but it brings some features never before seen in a controller.

Notably, the Aeon Pro borrows the outstanding "infinite battery" system from the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro line of gaming headsets . Instead of relying on a cable or dock to charge the controller, the Aeon Pro has two rechargeable batteries – one in the controller and another that charges in the base station. Like the Nova Pro, when one battery runs out of juice, you simply pop it out and swap it with the fully-charged one from the base station. In less than 10 seconds, your controller is fully juiced up and the previously depleted battery is tucked back in the dock to charge.

I'm a big believer in this "infinite" battery system. It's one of the most revolutionary features to come to gaming headsets and is the reason I continue to recommend the Arctis Nova Pro, so I'm thrilled to see SteelSeries implement it in a controller. Even better, the base station also serves as a dock for the controller, giving it a home to live on your desk or entertainment center when not in use.

The dock also solves another headache for players like me who game across multiple systems. The dock has separate USB-C connections for both Xbox and PC, and when both are plugged in, you can swap between them (and a third Bluetooth connection) on the controller itself. Unfortunately there's no PS5 or Switch 2 functionality here.

The one drawback to this system is it doesn't work great if your PC and Xbox aren't near each other. If they're in different rooms, or far enough that a wired connection from the base station to each device would be cumbersome, a simple dongle that you can unplug and take with you would be more convenient. It would be a lot more useful if it had PlayStation support, since your consoles likely all live with your TV, while PC is the wildcard that might be in another room.

The Aeon Pro packs in just about every high-end "pro-controller" feature on offer. Hall-effect thumbsticks join an Xbox-layout of ABXY buttons backed up by tactile switch connections. The triggers have two-stage Hall-effect sensors as well, while around back there's four paddles for additional inputs. All the buttons, bumpers, paddles, and even the D-pad, as well as the triggers when set to the short-throw position, offer a pleasing audible click.

Finally, there's a small OLED display above the Xbox button to show battery life and aid in configuration, whether that's just swapping between systems or full-on custom button remapping. It's a useful feature that takes the guesswork out of wondering which profile or custom button map you have active, though it's not quite advanced as the "has its own OS" capabilities of the totally over-engineered Genki Manta .

I spent most of my testing time slashing through corrupted fiends in the excellent new Onimusha: Way of the Sword , and the Aeon Pro served as an outstanding conduit for my mind-body-sword connection. Whether I was slashing and dodging or chaining together Issen counterattacks, the Aeon Pro felt excellent in hand and never failed to deliver my strikes.

All of this adds up to an excellent controller that is quickly becoming my go-to for anything that I don't need the Steam Controller 's trackpads. The biggest caveat of course is the price. At $260 it sits well above even other high-end "pro" controllers like the Turtle Beach Stealth Ultra and Asus ROG Raikiri II , but it does offer unique features never before seen in a controller.

I haven't spent enough time with the Aeon Pro yet to render final judgement, especially considering how expensive this thing is, so I'll be testing it more over the next week and will update this article with my final thoughts once I've fully put it through its paces.

articles.title: White House takes down 'Build the Wall' game after the Tetris Company complains | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Trump administration's short-lived arcade game "Build the Wall" is now nowhere to be found after the Tetris Company posted that it takes "copyright infringement very seriously."
articles.body:
A video game posted to the Trump administration’s website — one that closely resembled Tetris — has been taken down after the Tetris Company complained.

The White House recently took the unusual step of posting a number of arcade-style video games to its website. One of the more controversial was a game called “Build the Wall,” which reportedly mirrored Tetris’ gameplay, tasking players with stacking blocks of various shapes and sizes. Widely criticized as racist, the stated goal of the game was to build a wall in order to keep out a “zombie border siege.”

Not long after Build the Wall’s existence became public, the Tetris Company — which owns the rights to the original Tetris game — spoke out about it, clarifying that it had no role in its creation. “The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall,’” it said in an Instagram post , adding: “We take copyright infringement very seriously.”

The page for Build the Wall now returns a 404 error, meaning the page no longer exists. Kotaku first spotted that the game was no longer visible on the White House’s website. TechCrunch has reached out to the Trump administration for comment.

Still visible on the government’s website is a game called Rio Run , where players control a white male character whose goal is to deport as many immigrant characters as possible.

articles.title: AMC Theaters Is Broadcasting the 2026 Rocket League World Championship Finals at Select Cinemas Across the US
articles.summary: The 2026 Rocket League World Championship Finals will be broadcast at 50 AMC Theaters across the United States.
articles.body:
The 2026 Rocket League World Championship Finals will be broadcast at 50 AMC Theaters across the United States.

The Finals take place on Sunday, September 20. That day, fans can show up to participating AMC Theaters nationwide and catch the action on the big screen.

The competition will stream live from Dickies Arena in Fort Worth, Texas, where 20 teams will throw down for the chance to win $300,000 out of a staggering $1.2 million prize pool. The total broadcast will last approximately eight hours.

Rocket League - No Time To Die's Aston Martin Valhalla

Tickets are currently on sale at participating theaters, with adult tickets priced at $19.49 ($22.18 if booked online). Only a few of these theaters are showing the Finals, and tickets are selling out fast, so make sure to grab yours quickly if you want a front row seat to see who gets crowned the 15th Rocket League World Champions.

Most major esports tournaments are streamed on Twitch, with viewers receiving special drops that can be earned by simply watching on the platform. AMC Theaters has already thought of this, and is giving fans commemorative Rocket League tickets that include codes to redeem the drops that they would normally get watching the competition on Twitch.

“Such a big part of the magic of movie theatres is their ability to bring people together for unforgettable shared experiences, and a live event like the Rocket League World Championship is a great example of that," Ellen Copaken, SVP of Business Development for AMC Theatres, said in a press release. "We're excited to give fans the opportunity to watch esports' biggest stage unfold live on massive screens, surrounded by fellow Rocket League fans.”

A full list of the participating theaters can be found at the link embedded here.

This isn’t the first time an esports tournament has been shown at a theater; last year, the League of Legends Worlds Finals in Chengdu, China were shown in select theaters across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Riot did the same for the Valorant Champions Paris Finals , which also screened in certain cinemas throughout EMEA.

AMC’s decision to broadcast esports is the latest unique move from the brand after it founded a film distribution company to help get smaller films into theaters. With small-budget projects like Obsession and Markiplier’s Iron Lung proving to be hits at the box office, AMC is stepping in to capitalize on the trend and bring art to the masses.

articles.title: Netflix Orders Lonesome Dove TV Series From East of Eden Showrunners
articles.summary: Netflix is adapting Larry McMurtry’s iconic Western novel Lonesome Dove into a new TV series from East of Eden co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart.
articles.body:
Netflix has ordered a series retelling of Larry McMurtry's Pulitzer Prize-winning Western novel Lonesome Dove.

The project will reteam the streaming service with East of Eden co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart. Teton Ridge Entertainment owns the film and TV rights to McMurtry's Lonesome Dove book series.

McMurtry's 1985 bestseller follows former Texas Rangers-turned-cowboys Augustus "Gus" McRae and Woodrow Call, who embark on a fateful 3000-mile cattle drive to Montana, encountering a variety of frontier dangers along the way.

CBS adapted it as a blockbuster TV miniseries in 1989 starring Robert Duvall , Tommy Lee Jones, Danny Glover, Rick Schroder, Diane Lane, Robert Urich, Anjelica Huston, Steve Buscemi, Chris Cooper, Frederic Forrest, and Glenne Headly.

“After our singular experience on East of Eden, we are thrilled to be teaming with Netflix again, along with Teton Ridge Entertainment, to bring Larry McMurtry’s western classic to life,” Kazan and Stuart said in a statement (via Deadline ).

“We come to this material with love and respect, and can’t wait to hit the trail with Gus and Call and the rest of these beloved characters. Yee-haw.”

According to Deadline, Kazan and Stuart will executive produce Lonesome Dove with Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge Entertainment; Jon Jashni; late McMurtry’s longtime creative partner Diana Ossana; Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate.

articles.title: Hands on: Tianji: Shadow of the Ancients
articles.summary: Hands on: Tianji: Shadow of the Ancients
articles.body:
If Square Enix's ongoing success is any measure, HD-2D-style games have found a sizable audience and pumped fresh blood into this nostalgic offshoot of the RPG genre. It's not just JRPGs getting in on the turn-based action, however. Taipei-based developer Justdan have announced their own lovingly crafted RPG, Tianji: Shadow of the Ancients: itself a tribute to RPGs of yesteryear, albeit with a distinctly mainland-Asian twist.

Instead of magic, the reality-adjacent world of Tianji is set during the Tang Dynasty, in a land powered by Qi energy. Practitioners of Eastern martial arts will be familiar with the basic concept, but for the uninitiated, Qi energy resides in all living things. The trick is to harness Qi energy and use it for powerful, mystical means. So, yeah, it's still sort of magic - but the roots are a little different here.

Our main character, Shangguan Shuo, is dealt a rough hand early on and struck with amnesia by the nefarious Xuanxin Order; it's the classic adventurer's downfall. These folks really need to keep their helmets on at all times. Regardless, his head trauma kicks off a journey to rebuild his memory and uncover the reason for the strange voice in his head that is causing him to question his identity.

Along the way we meet a cast of characters eager to join your side and throw their lives into harm's way, turn after turn after turn. That's very noble of them.

Tianji: Shadow of the Ancients offers a charming blend of light exploration and deeper turn-based combat mechanics. Unlike Square Enix's pixellated sprite character rendering, Tianji's characters are razor-sharp 2D chibi-style interpretations of their more realistically proportioned key art likenesses. Still, they are imbued with plenty of little animated touches, emoting here and there throughout the in-engine cutscenes. Other cutscenes play out in a blend of ink-on-canvas inspired styles and more conventional 3D scenes.

Rendered via Unreal Engine 5, the world is presented in a combination of smaller 3D villages, towns, caves, forests and mountains. The camera tracks from a set distance, creating plenty of tasty depth of field effects.

The formula may seem familiar and the first couple hours are easy enough to dive into even if you're not particularly into turn-based RPGs, finding them slow and tedious. Personally, the deliberate pace of a turn-based RPG is where I find a lot of the charm, but results may vary, as they say.

To that end, the developers wisely made a few modern accommodations to speed up the gameplay for the ADHD-HD2D generation. Battles can be sped up - up to 2x the normal speed, and after levelling up a bit, you can automatically defeat lower levelled foes without transitioning into battle.

Progression follows a similar philosophy: a vertical skill tree with enough branches to feel like a real choice rather than a formality and skills that combine across the whole party instead of staying locked to whoever's swinging the sword that turn. Most of them lean into elemental strengths and weaknesses, too, which adds a layer of actual strategy on top of the button-mashing instinct turn-based combat usually beats out of you. One skill on show, Scattered Stars II, fires three hits at random targets and, on a critical hit, just goes again for free. That's a good preview of how deep the tree might get once you're a dozen hours in.

You'll also pick up companions along the way (see: the noble idiots mentioned earlier, throwing themselves into harm's way on your behalf) and each comes with a personal side story and a skill nobody else has. Spend time with them and that skill improves, picking up things like weapon enhancement, cooking up buffs at camp, or trading away items you don't need for ones you do.

It's an old trick - party members that get better the more you actually use them, but it's a good one, and it gives you a reason to run the B-team once in a while instead of sticking with the strongest three forever.

Between fights, those Qi leylines aren't just flavour text either. They cut across the overworld map and, from the look of it, are tied to why this game is so preoccupied with its own scenery. Wander off the main road and there are hidden bosses, side quests and dungeons for the taking, which is the traditional reward for ignoring the quest marker in any RPG worth its salt.

Tianji: Shadow of the Ancients is currently pencilled in for 2027, heading to Steam, both generations of Switch and PS5. That's a wide net for a game this specific in its influences and a long way off besides.

Early days, then, but between the ink-wash scenery, an amnesiac lead with a voice in his head that isn't his own and a combat system that actually seems to want you paying attention, I'm cautiously optimistic about this one.

IGN was a guest of BiliBili for this preview event.

articles.title: Apparent Steam Leak Reveals Persona 6 and Kingdom Hearts 4 Achievements, Unannounced Games
articles.summary: Achievements for various upcoming games have been made public as part of a significant Steam leak.
articles.body:
Achievements for various upcoming games have been made public as part of a significant Steam leak.

Spoiler-filled achievements for Persona 6 and Kingdom Hearts 4 , among many others, appeared on achievement tracking website Exophase. In the case of Kingdom Hearts 4, the achievements reveal unannounced worlds. The Persona 6 achievements hint at plot points.

Little is known about Persona 6, which was announced during June’s Xbox Games Showcase with the teaser, below.

We do know it's a day-one Game Pass title, though, and that it is due out on Xbox Series X and S, PlayStation 5 and PC via Steam. Here’s the official blurb:

“Persona 6 brings everything beloved about the series into a bold new story. The signature blend of heartfelt daily life and pulse-pounding supernatural adventure returns, wrapped around a completely fresh, standalone story and a new cast of characters. Whether you've been with the series since the beginning or this is your very first Persona experience, you belong here!”

Square Enix has announced just one Kingdom Hearts 4 world so far: Coco. Last month, Kingdom Hearts 4 co-director Tai Yasue and series creator Tetsuya Nomura assured fans that it is a "100% thing" the game will not be delayed past its late 2027 launch window.

Kingdom Hearts 4 Extended Gameplay Trailer | D23 2026

The owner of Exophase blamed this leak on Steam owner Valve. “Seems like a possible screw up on Valve's end, a bunch of games with achievements that should be private are accessible through the API right now and that's why they got scanned into the site,” x3sphere said in a post on ResetEra . “I usually never see games without an actual name pop up with achievements, yet over the past hour or so a bunch have (when there's an unknown name we just set it to the AppID).”

Also included in the leak are a number of unannounced games, such as a Steam release for Capcom’s much-loved Nintendo 3DS game, Professor Layton vs. Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney. There’s also an unannounced Nickelodeon game, unannounced Telltale Games The Walking Dead Collection, and an unannounced Tetris game. Gematsu has a roundup.

articles.title: Anthropic Safety Researcher Says There's a More Than 10% Chance AI 'Could Kill All Humans' Within the Next Decade
articles.summary: An Anthropic safety researcher has said there is a greater than 10% chance that AI “could kill all humans” within the next decade, and admitted there is no coordinated plan to prevent it from happening.
articles.body:
An Anthropic safety researcher has said there is a greater than 10% chance that AI “could kill all humans” within the next decade, and admitted there is no coordinated plan to prevent it from happening.

U.S. company Anthropic, headed up by Dario Amodei, develops the Large Language Model (LLM) Claude and conducts AI research. Yesterday, one of the company’s researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced his resignation on X / Twitter , accusing both ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Anthropic of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

“Neither company is acting responsible,” Coxon, who previously worked at OpenAI, said. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he continued. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

Coxon said that staff at OpenAI, headed up by Sam Altman, “have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes,” which is why work to rapidly improve its AI models continues despite the risks. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first," he insisted. “They believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk.”

“Accepting this race and entering the ‘endgame’ is a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company’s Slack. Attempting to speedrun alignment should require extraordinary confidence that there are no better trajectories available.”

Coxon went on to say he was optimistic about the potential for coordination, but doubted AI companies were on track to prevent a global race, “which may require costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities.”

He ended his statement by urging AI lab researchers to consider what they were doing. “Do you want to kick off a superintelligent RL run without a rigorous understanding of its mind?” he asked. “Should you put your head down because ‘it’s happening anyway’ - or take this moment to call for different conditions?”

Coxon’s statement has sent shockwaves throughout social media, sparking alarm and a string of mainstream headlines. But then it was backed up by Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s ‘Alignment Science’ lead, who added an even starker warning.

“Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he said . “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Remarkably, Hubinger pointed to Anthropic’s latest Risk Report, in which the company said it believes the risk from present models is “low,” rather than suggest a pause that might help prevent the extinction of humankind. “What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought,” he added.

The comments come after the Financial Times reported that Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute, one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

This summer has seen a number of worrying developments that show how AI has become hard to control, even by those who create it. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have all disclosed hacks carried out by their autonomous AI agents. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki recently called for "extreme caution" over AI progress, warning more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future.”

However, the U.S. government has shown no sign of stepping in to force restrictions upon or even suggest a slowing down of AI development. In fact, quite the opposite. Earlier this month, the Trump administration backed OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence. “The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally… As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence,'” the government's brief said, referencing an executive order President Donald Trump signed last year.

Meanwhile, despite dire warnings coming from staff at Anthropic and OpenAI, neither company seems willing to pull the plug. Coxon and Hubinger’s statements have sparked extreme concern across social media, with some expressing disbelief that work to improve AI is continuing even with such significant risk.

“Hey! Here’s a novel idea… could we just f***ing not kill ourselves due to an insatiable appetite for power and money?” one person said. “Crazy take: maybe you shouldn’t be allowed to gamble with our lives?” another added. “If I literally claimed that there was a 10% chance that I was building something that would kill people, the FBI would have me arrested. How are you not in jail?” another asked.

Photo Illustration by Dominika Zarzycka/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images.

articles.title: No Law Looks Like the Deus Ex Successor I’ve Been Waiting For
articles.summary: No Law looks like the Deus Ex successor I’ve been waiting for.
articles.body:
We stepped into Port Desire’s bustling street market to conduct a simple, albeit grisly experiment: How many people can we make explode into bits of blood and pulp with a single gunshot?

To achieve this messy masterpiece, we walked slowly into the middle of a tightly packed crowd to find the optimal spot for maximum impact. A stasis grenade was then thrown into the mix, suspending every unfortunate body within its blast radius in a vibrating, temporal state. Such is the kinetic energy built up by the event that all it took was a single headshot for a chain reaction to begin, each subsequent body erupting into wet chunks of bone and organ as the market transformed into a human popcorn maker. In turn, this set off a nearby box of ammunition to continue the carnage, firing off extra bullets in all directions to claim yet more victims. This is only one example of how No Law’s malleable systems can be bent to your own sick desires. This could, maybe just, be the Deus Ex successor I’ve been waiting for.

When not painted with the insides of its civilian population, Port Desire is a vibrant, neon metropolis. Think Cyberpunk’s Night City crossed with Dishonored 2’s Karnaca, its Mediterranean-like vegetation fighting back to reclaim the land as vines wind up glass, steel, and concrete architecture. It’s home to Grey Harker, an ex-military man who’s just trying to lead a quiet retirement. As is the way, though, trouble finds its way to his door, and he’s left with no choice but to invite violence back into his life and clean up this city once and for good. With a body built like Reacher’s and the deductive mind of Deckard, he’s your vehicle for navigating this world, and you can use it however you see fit.

At first glance, No Law might look like Cyberpunk 2077, but to be frank, so will any first-person sci-fi shooter set in a futuristic metropolis that follows in the footsteps of William Gibson’s genre-defining cyberpunk fiction. But there's an important distinction between No Law and 2077. This isn’t an RPG; it’s an immersive sim shooter in the mold of genre pioneer Deus Ex. No Law’s city is smaller than the average open world, but incredibly dense. There’s a sense of verticality begging to be explored, from dingy, rat-filled subways to rooftops high above. But these layers aren’t just set dressing — each tier can be scaled, especially once the ability to perform cybernetically enhanced superjumps is unlocked.

But for all the sci-fi tech and gadgetry on show, it’s still the human mind that is predominantly being pushed to its limits, and your ability to consider every possible approach to an objective. This is best showcased in a simple mission. The task, in theory, was simple: gain access to a second-floor room of an apartment complex. But in order to do so, we’d need to deal with a group of gang members, a surly, unhelpful receptionist, and a locked door. To show the full range of options available when faced with such a series of obstacles, developer Neon Giant walked me through the infiltration in two distinctly different ways.

First, we went for the sneaky option. Harker may be the size of a small tank, but that doesn’t mean he isn’t well-versed in the art of stealth. To circumvent the gun-toting gang members gathered outside the front door of the building, we searched for an alternative way in. This led us around the side, where we clambered up to some high ground and scuttled behind our would-be attackers, dropping down silently before sneaking through an open door. A turn to the right brought us face-to-face with a grumpy concierge dressed in a terrible flower-patterned suit. I could tell he smelled the opposite of the petals adorning his jacket, but his attitude stank even more.

He wasn’t going to let us pass through to the staircase, which led up towards our goal. And so, we were left with a choice to make. The quickest way would be to offer a bribe and cough up enough cash to make him turn a blind eye. But we didn’t want to give him the satisfaction of earning anything from us other than a powerful feeling of disdain, so we searched around the lobby area until we found a password written on a piece of paper attached to a notice board. Just that bit of patience and a willingness to search for an alternative solution saved us a whole lot of money.

Up the stairs we went, making sure to sneak past a couple of enemies patrolling the landing. The next puzzle to solve was how to get into the room that was the whole reason for us being here. The door was, predictably, locked, and we didn’t have any lockpicking gear with us, so another way in had to be found. So, we checked out the next-door neighbour, who had conveniently left their door ajar before falling asleep inside. We made sure to crouch and move quietly so as not to wake them, stealing some of their food and reading their personal diary while we were at it. Once full of nutrients and new info, we spotted a vent leading into the next room. And so, following in Batman’s tradition of oversized men somehow nimbly crawling through ducts not meant for them, Harker squeezed his way into the room at the heart of our objective.

But of course, this could’ve gone an entirely much bloodier way. We reloaded the save and started all over again, this time intent on causing chaos. That group of troublemakers loitering outside? One throw of the aforementioned stasis grenade and a round of ammunition quickly turned them into chunks. That awfully dressed, sweaty meat sack of a receptionist? A swift bullet to the head meant he had no more use for passwords. Perhaps the most interesting change this time around, though, was that this new run-through took place at night, and so the two gang members upstairs now exhibited different behaviours than when we snuck past them during daylight. One was leaning over a bannister, so we walked up behind them and sharply snapped their neck. The other lay asleep in bed – not that such slumber could stop us from taking out our pistol and making sure he’d never wake again, though.

This time, getting into the target room was much easier, thanks to this save having dropped a lockpicking device in our pocket and enough skill points to upgrade our breaking-and-entering ability and make our way in. Incidentally, this time we entered, items had fallen from shelves and lay strewn across the floor due to the impact of the stasis grenade explosion outside just moments earlier. It’s another great example of how reactive the world of No Law is to your actions.

It’s a city packed with detail, too. Outside of the quest, we took time to stroll around its streets and take in some of the sights. Developed by a small team of just 24 members, it really is remarkable how good it all looks and sounds. Grimy, yet bright. Modern, yet lived in. Just browsing around a local shop, I couldn’t quite believe how much work had gone into making every item on its shelves — all of which can be added to your basket and consumed for a variety of buffs and bonuses. This is an open world that promises big, explosive moments, but one that isn’t forgetting about the small details, either. Each drink bottle and piece of food packaging has been handcrafted — Neon Giant isn’t a team interested in letting generative AI replace its artistry.

Of course, as is the immersive sim way, there are multiple ways to procure these items, too. You can be a normal citizen and simply shop here, filling up your inventory at the expense of emptying your wallet. You could steal the items, but the shopkeeper will remember and not be very happy to see you next time you set foot in there. Or, you can do what we did and wait until night, find the key to the back door, and sneak in while the owner is asleep. This is a persistent world, too, so when a door’s lock is cracked, this method of entry will remain available for the rest of your playthrough.

One thing that’s as of yet unclear is if Neon Giant has the storytelling chops to fully engross me in this world — neither the slice I saw here nor the studio’s previous sci-shooter, The Ascent, have been narratively focused — but it’s the promise of the stories I’ll be able to tell through the tools handed to me in No Law that has me most excited. Yes, Deus Ex: Human Revolution tells a great tale of corporate ethics and conspiracy worthy of the wonderful sci-fi scenery it's set against, and Dishonored 2’s revenge drama stemming from a royal coup is highly engaging, but it’s the moments of magic I created within those stories that live longest in my memory. It’s the possibility of this, and all of the numerous other anecdotes No Law promises to offer, that has me most excited. That, and seeing if I can set a new record for the number of heads exploded by a single bullet.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Preorders Are Finally Live in the UK
articles.summary: Preorders for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake are now live in the UK on Nintendo Switch 2, featuring exclusive bonuses and a textured foil sleeve.
articles.body:
While those in the UK had to wait a little longer than others , preorders for the highly anticipated remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time are now available on Nintendo Switch 2 .

The game is available to preorder from Smyths for £54.99 , while Nintendo is charging £58.99 for the game as a physical copy, and £49.99 for the digital edition.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Spiritual Stones are also available as a free bonus when preordering the game from Nintendo's UK Store .

You can also preorder with an Ocarina of Time Pin for a small additional cost: £61.98 for the physical edition or £52.98 for the digital edition .

Preorders are also currently available at Game and ShopTo . We're waiting on Amazon, Argos, and Currys to go live next in the UK.

Also, as a reminder, all copies of the game in its first print run will include a "textured foil cover sleeve" that is shiny . It sounds simple, but plenty of fans are going mad for it.

I've also had it confirmed that Smyths will definitely have the foiled sleeve as part of its preorder campaign, if that's your prefered place to shop.

While it's still easy to get hold of Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, Zelda's 40th Anniversary console and accessories are a different story .

It's sold out at Nintendo and Smyths right now ( which is a similar story globally ), but we're still awaiting news from Amazon, Argos, Currys, and other major UK retailers to see if there another opportunity to preorder.

What Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a full remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 original, with completely overhauled graphics designed to bring the classic adventure up to modern standards.

Rather than adding a large amount of new content, Nintendo describes the game as a "faithful interpretation" of the original built for modern hardware. There are some additions, however, including more dialogue for the characters Link encounters throughout his adventure, giving them a little more personality.

The remake also introduces several quality-of-life improvements, including a fully free-roaming camera, a dedicated jump button, a roll/run button, and motion-control aiming. Cutscenes will feature full voice acting, while the Zelda Notes app can also be used alongside the game.

There's even an audio input option that lets you hum the game's songs, allowing Link to play them in-game. A new "Threads of Time" menu will also recap your progress and highlight your current objective, making it easier to keep track of where you've been and what you need to do next.

You can usually find Robert lost in open-world RPG games like Elden Ring and Cyberpunk 2077. Outside of gaming, his passions include reading comics (especially Superman, Batman, and Spider-Man), taking photos, and keeping up with the latest in film and TV.

His primary coverage focuses on tracking down the best gaming deals and diving into the fast-paced world of Trading Card Games (TCGs). He regularly covers everything from the latest releases in Pokémon TCG and the most expensive cards to comprehensive Magic: The Gathering buying guides . As a massive Doctor Who fan, he also keeps a close eye on physical media deals like Doctor Who Blu-ray preorders , and occasionally steps away from commerce to contribute reviews for the site, such as his review of Doctor Who's latest season .

articles.title: GAA Integration: Tom Ryan refutes claims of misogyny in 'strongest possible terms'
articles.summary: GAA director general Tom Ryan says the organisation's commitment to integration remains "firm and absolute" in the wake of comments made by former Irish president Dr Mary McAleese.
articles.body:
GAA director general Tom Ryan has said the organisation's commitment to integration remains "firm and absolute" in the wake of comments made by former Irish president Dr Mary McAleese.

In February 2024, the Gaelic Athletic Association [GAA], Ladies Gaelic Football Association [LGFA] and the Camogie Association announced an intention to merge into one body.

Dr McAleese resigned from her position as chair of the committee tasked with overseeing the amalgamation on Tuesday and said she was "devastated" that the stated target of 2027 would not he met. She added she was "dubious" of the GAA's commitment to integration.

Ryan told RTE Radio's Morning Ireland , external that he "can't accept" the idea that the missed target is a result of misogyny.

"I would refute that in the strongest possible terms," he said.

"I accept in the course of a project like this there will be different perspectives, and different points of view and that's fine but I can't accept that as a charge.

"I'm very, very proud to be part of the GAA. I'm proud of what it is and does.

"It's an inclusive organisation, it's a family-orientated organisation, it's a progressive organisation, and in leadership terms both nationally and locally, there are countless women who play a huge part in guiding and driving the organisation."

'GAA integration target will be very hard to meet'

Begley calls for 'positivity' on Gaelic games merger

Ryan said the original target of 2027 had proven to be "a little bit too ambitious" but that integration will still happen through a "phased implementation".

He added: "I don't see a future for us as a standalone organisation, promoting and offering male sports only. Our future is together.

"We will be far stronger as a combined organisation. I believe that. The GAA believes that. I know my colleagues in ladies football and camogie believe that.

"All we are looking at here is we've missed a deadline, our own deadline. Our job now is to just recast things in light of that, to learn from that and push ahead."

articles.title: Andrew Garfield Delivers a Fierce Performance as a Peasant Rebel Fighting English Oppression in The Uprising, an Uneven, Gritty Historical Drama
articles.summary: Read our review of The Uprising, the historical drama starring Andrew Garfield as a peasant rebel and proto-Robin Hood defying English tyranny in a gritty fight for freedom.
articles.body:
Writer-director Paul Greengrass’ The Uprising is a visceral and kinetic but uneven chronicle of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in England, anchored by the ever-reliable Andrew Garfield’s moving performance as a mournful farmer who helps spark a rebellion that seeks to improve the lives of the common folk. As he has done in Bloody Sunday and United 93 , Greengrass focuses on everyday people who get caught up in tragic historic events. The Uprising, though, can’t quite find the balance between the "big picture" events it’s depicting and those smaller-scale, more focused docudramas.

Called simply Ploughman, Garfield’s protagonist feverishly works the land every day just to eke out the barest living. His small farm, which belongs to a local lord, is also the resting place of his late wife and two children. He basically has nothing left, a crushing state shared by many of his neighbors. Set at a time when the people are gripped by immense grief – England had lost roughly half its population to the Black Death – their pain fuels not only their fury at the powers-that-be but also their hope that God can miraculously deliver them from their misery.

With problems at home and wars abroad, the government is in need of more funds – the lords are unwilling to let the merchant class enter their ranks and the Church won’t spend anymore – so they enact a heavy new tax that guts the commoners. Collection methods are so brutal and dehumanizing that, sparked by Ploughman’s violent outburst, the peasants finally snap. Ploughman and his neighbors soon join a peasant army led by Cosmo Jarvis’ brawny ex-soldier Wat Tyler and Jamie Bell’s fiery renegade priest John Ball. (Both Tyler and Ball are real figures while the Ploughman is fictional.)

They march towards London not to overthrow King Richard II – their quarrel is more with his council of cads who are really in charge – but to petition him for sweeping reforms. (The King, one must remember, was thought to be divinely chosen, so fealty to him is also showing devotion to God.) But the rage that such long-term oppression has fostered in the peasants – exemplified by Thomasin McKenzie’s fervent Alyce, who seeks to inflict her suffering on her perceived enemies – ultimately explodes into sheer anarchy.

By showing such a savage mob mentality take hold, Greengrass challenges the justness of the peasants’ actions, which muddies one’s feelings about the titular uprising. History is never clean and Greengrass wants to show that, but the film makes you doubt your sympathy for its underdogs once the bloodletting erupts into utter chaos on the streets of London.

Shot in the cinéma vérité style that’s become a Greengrass hallmark, the filmmaker immerses the viewer in the grimy, relentlessly miserable life of medieval serfdom, achieving the you-are-there effect so well that you’re thankful Smell-O-Vision doesn’t exist. Yet Greengrass repeatedly pulls the viewer out of this historical realism by cutting to jarring digital aerial shots swooping over London – attempts to demonstrate the scale of the revolt – images that seem, at best, filmed by a Ye Olde Drone or, worse, AI-generated.

The cast is uniformly solid, with the film’s rogues gallery brought to life by a murderer’s row of British character actors – Tom Hollander as Treasurer Robert Hales, Stephen Dillane as Archbishop Simon Sudbury, Stanley Townsend as Chief Justice Belknap, and an unrecognizable Jonny Lee Miller as London’s Mayor William Walworth – all of whom play their characters with varying degrees of haughty cruelty.

But these men are in the service of teenage King Richard II, portrayed with nuance and complexity by Woody Norman. Richard, who may have a personality disorder of some kind, is bedeviled by nightmares and utterly petrified with piety — before he finally takes charge of his fate with a brutal efficiency that stuns even his own mother, Joan, Countess of Kent (an understated Katherine Waterston). The Uprising initially generates some sympathy for the King until, of course, the little shit pisses away any such good will.

The Uprising also depicts the bureaucracy that keeps the engine of oppression operating, particularly the paperwork that can either expose the rebels’ identities or serve as their literal ticket to a better life. I’ve never seen a suspense set-piece before where a roomful of scribes with quill pens must furiously copy dozens of charters in order to meet a crucial deadline. Write fast! No, faster!

There’s plenty of tension in the final act – which also takes significant creative liberties with the events that transpired at Smithfield on June 15, 1381 – but that’s also where Greengrass’ breathlessly-paced film loses its footing, straining to turn history on its head with a Braveheart-worthy happy ending. The final scenes, which would be at home in a Mel Gibson or Robin Hood movie -- it wasn't known to be a Rise of Robin Hood movie at the time I screened the film and Garfield's character is never referred to as such -- end The Uprising on an awkward note rather than the crowd-pleasing one that seemed intended.

articles.title: No Man's Sky 10th Anniversary Cosmos Update Actually Updates Space, Lets Players Finally Reach Stars
articles.summary: No Man’s Sky developer Hello Games has continued the relentless pace of updates for the space game, this time releasing a 10th anniversary patch called Cosmos.
articles.body:
No Man’s Sky developer Hello Games has continued the relentless pace of updates for the space game, this time releasing a 10th anniversary patch called Cosmos.

Hello Games chief Sean Murray said Cosmos is one of No Man Sky’s “biggest and craziest” updates ever, as it actually updates space.

“No Man’s Sky is often referred to as ‘a Space Game,’ it’s a huge part of our game, but we’ve never really updated space since release,” Murray said. “In most sci-fi games, space is just an empty void. With Cosmos we wondered - can we make space feel truly alive? And could we make space feel more like home? What if you could own a Space Station? If you could build star bases, and create alliances with other players.”

No Man's Sky 7.0 Cosmos Update Screenshots

Additions include a Star Map, huge space hulks, new space outposts, bio-wrecks, asteroid belts, free-floating orbital bases, space station ownership (one of the most requested features since launch), alliances, and — finally — the ability to actually reach the star at the center of players’ own star system.

Hello Games has launched an expedition alongside the Cosmos update, called Our Journey Continues! It includes milestones that represent one of the 40 major updates since No Man’s Sky launched in 2016. “It is like a museum of each update, unlocking the features of each update as we added them, along with a spacelog of interesting facts and developers commentary for each update,” Murray explained. “It’s been a real joy to revisit some of those moments for us.”

Patch notes are below, courtesy of Hello Games.

No Man’s Sky 7.0 Cosmos update patch notes:

Star Map: Warping to a system now, your first action will often be a quick scan of the new star map to reveal a whole new array of space points of interest, each of which unlocks whole new strands of missions and exploration.

Hulks: There are huge “space hulks”, which can be stripped and salvaged. The physics gravity gun can be used to pull chunks of metal from these wrecks, and can be thrown to a new tractor beam fitted to your ship. Become too greedy, and tear too much from a hulk, and it may begin to meltdown and explode. Scanning first for the highest value rewards is the smart move.

Outposts: Perhaps you take your new rewards to one of the new space outposts, to trade with alien lifeforms. Here you can buy maps, get information about the area and take on new missions from its inhabitants.

Bio-wrecks: Beware though, some of these facilities have been overwhelmed by biological hazards, and may need to be cleared out and reclaimed carefully.

Asteroid Belts: Gorgeous asteroid belts of rock and ice formations boast a large array of valuable crystal resources. Some rare asteroids are large enough to land on and even build a star base on.

Orbital Bases: Why limit yourself to a base on an asteroid? Free-floating modular bases can be built ANYWHERE in space. Build your own truck stop for star ships, orbital restaurant, or military outpost. There’s something incredibly special about floating in space, planets looming large below you, watching the universe go by.

Space Station Ownership: This must be our most requested feature since launch… finally players can buy the space station for themselves! Build and decorate it both inside and externally, and some wild creativity is possible. You can create your own themed Station, as your own clubhouse and have friends come and visit.

Alliances: Perhaps that Station then becomes the place where you found your own ALLIANCE to which you can invite all players to join your new society. As an alliance, you can work together to build a networked empire of different stations and rise the new leaderboards to compete for the largest, richest or most prominent alliance.

Reach Stars: The center of the solar system is the sun, and finally players can try to undertake a perilous journey to reach the center of their own star system!

articles.summary: Preorders are live for Young Link and Young Zelda amiibo from the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake. But they're selling out fast.
articles.body:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Nintendo Switch 2 is coming in November, and when preorders went live , we saw tons of traffic a preorders go through. Suffice to say this is going to be a huge game. To go along with it, Nintendo is also releasing a pair of amiibo figures: Young Link and Young Zelda. Both cost $24.99 and have gone up for preorder at several retailers. However, they’re selling out fast, so don’t hesitate to lock in a preorder if you find one in stock . Note: these amiibo are selling out quickly, so if you see one in stock and you want it, I’d grab it ASAP. I’ll keep updating this article as the amiibo go live at new retailers.

Scanning these amiibo while playing the Ocarina of Time remake gets you an in-game mask “that evokes the graphical style of the original game.” Which is to say, the masks look angular and low-poly. But in a charming way.

As for the inspiration for these amiibo figures, Young Link and Young Zelda meet relatively early in the original N64 game. After leaving his forest home and crossing the vast expanse of Hyrule Field, young Link sneaks past some castle guards and finds himself in a courtyard. That’s where he meets young Zelda, whom he’s never met, but who has seen him in a prophecy.
